Part 0

How to use this pack

Start here. The ten-minute version first, then a reading plan for the week before the deadline.

Your situation in one box@@m0-situation@@

18 Oct
Applications close (2026), via SEO London. Rank six teams 1 to 6.
6 teams
PE and Global Impact, Real Estate, Infrastructure, Capital Markets, Client Solutions (your first choice), Capstone.
6 Jun to 29 Jul
The 2027 internship, eight weeks in the London office.

No interview is scheduled yet, and the interviewers are not known. So this pack does two jobs: it helps you write an application nobody else could write this week, and it prepares you for interviews that could follow within weeks. When names and dates arrive, use the checklist in the interview part.

The ten-minute emergency version@@m0-ten@@

If you read nothing else, read these ten points. Each is expanded, with sources, later in the pack.

  1. What KKR is. A listed alternative asset manager: it invests clients' money in private equity, private credit, infrastructure and real estate, and owns an insurer, Global Atlantic. $796.5bn of assets under management at 30 June 2026 [S1] CONFIRMED.
  2. Who pays KKR. Its clients (limited partners): pensions, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments, family offices and, increasingly, wealthy individuals. They pay management fees and a share of profits (carried interest).
  3. What KCS is. The team that raises and looks after that money: formed in 2009, 300+ people, split into relationship management and product/strategy management [S103, S141] CONFIRMED. KKR's words: it exists to "connect the dots" across all of KKR's businesses [S141].
  4. The three client channels. Institutions, Family Capital and Global Wealth. Private wealth is now 18% of KKR's AUM, ahead of pensions at 14% [S71] CONFIRMED. The wealth products are the evergreen K-Series, which grew from $6bn (2023) to $42bn (June 2026) [S72, S73].
  5. Why KCS works with Capital Markets. KKR can underwrite a deal and syndicate co-investment to clients through KCM; KCS brings the clients [S70]. In Europe one Partner, Mark Danzey, heads both KCM and Institutional Client Solutions [S156] CONFIRMED.
  6. Why KKR is built this way. One firm, one P&L, one compensation pool [S5]; employees own about 30% of the stock [S3]. So the client team can sell what fits the client, not what one team needs to fill INFERRED.
  7. The year so far. Record fundraising pace: $305bn raised since the start of 2024 against a $300bn target [S76]; Global Infrastructure Investors V closed at $19.2bn in August 2026, KKR's largest infrastructure fund [S176].
  8. The awkward facts. A proposed $250m DOJ settlement over merger filings (Aug 2026) [S205]; K-FIT paid about 80% of redemption requests in Q1 2026, then 100% in Q2 [S338]; founders' control ends by 31 Dec 2026 [S2]. Know them; state them neutrally.
  9. Where KKR does not lead. Blackstone and Apollo are larger, Blackstone leads private wealth by a wide margin, and in-house capital markets is not unique [S213, S215, S220]. Never overclaim.
  10. Your answer. "KCS is the team that has to understand all of KKR. KKR is built for that seat. I want to learn the whole firm by explaining it honestly to the people who fund it." Then one personal example of explaining something or keeping a commitment.

How the pack is organised, and its companion@@m0-map@@

This is the complete pack: the firm, all six London teams and how they link, the industry, the rules, the news, the interview and the scenarios. Its companion, the KCS Deep Dive, goes much further on Client Solutions: the team's history, products, channels, a reconstructed org chart, the role decoded line by line and a KCS-specific question bank and scenario playbook. How to read the markers@@m0-read@@

[S12] points to row S12 in the source table (Part 15). Every non-obvious fact has one.

CONFIRMED primary source or two credible outlets.
REPORTED one credible source.
INFERRED the author's reasoning from sourced facts.

Key term

Definitions in plain English.

Say this

Lines you can use.

Don't say this

Traps and overclaims.

Your opinion goes here

Where to form a view.

Source uncertain

Thin or conflicting evidence.

The rule that matters most

Only say a number in an interview if you can name where it came from. "According to KKR's second-quarter release..." is more impressive than a precise figure without a source, and it protects you if the interviewer has a newer number.

@@m1@@
Part 1

The internship decoded, the six teams mapped, and how they link

Every line of the advert explained, each team made concrete, and one map that shows how money, deals and stories move between them.

You are ranking six teams you have never sat in. This part gives you a working picture of each one: what it does on a Tuesday, who it talks to, what it hands to the others, and what it would want from you. Then it puts all six on one map. If you understand the map, you can answer "why this team?" for any of them, and you can explain why Client Solutions (KCS) sits at the centre of it.

How to read the tags

CONFIRMED means a primary source (KKR filings, kkr.com, KKR job posts, Companies House) or two good outlets. REPORTED means one credible source. INFERRED is reasoning from the facts, mostly mine. [Advert] is the internship text you were given. Source IDs like [S175] point to the source list at the back of the pack.

1. The advert, decoded line by line@@m1-advert@@

The advert has seven building blocks. Each one tells you something different about what KKR will test. Figure 1 shows the blocks and what you should prepare for each.

Block 1: "A leading global investment firm that offers alternative asset management as well as capital markets and insurance solutions"

This is KKR's standard boilerplate. It maps to KKR's three reporting segments: Asset Management (five business lines: Private Equity, Real Assets, Credit and Liquid Strategies, Capital Markets, Principal Activities), Insurance (Global Atlantic) and Strategic Holdings [S1, S2] CONFIRMED. Notice what comes first: asset management, not "private equity". Traditional private equity was over 70% of AUM in 2010 and under 25% at the end of 2025 [S2] CONFIRMED. The phrase "patient and disciplined investment approach, employing world-class people, and supporting growth in its portfolio companies and communities" is word for word the sentence in every KKR earnings release [S1] CONFIRMED.

Don't say this

"KKR is a private equity firm." Say "a global investment firm with asset management, insurance and strategic holdings". That is KKR's own framing [S1, S12] CONFIRMED.

Blocks 3 and 4: the teams and the common duty line

The advert names seven teams: Capital Markets, Capstone, KKR Client Solutions, Global Impact, Infrastructure, Private Equity and Real Estate. You rank six, because Global Impact sits inside the Private Equity choice. Then comes one sentence that applies to everybody: interns will be "involved in helping identify attractive investment themes and opportunities, synthesizing industry and market data and analysing potential investments" [Advert].

Read that carefully. Even the client-facing team (KCS) and the operations team (Capstone) are told they will work on investment themes. In KCS, a "theme" is what you pitch: why infrastructure, why now, why Europe INFERRED. In Capstone it is where the operating upside is. So every candidate, whatever the first choice, needs one investment idea they can explain and defend. KKR's head of talent acquisition says KKR wants candidates who "understand how the macro environment is affecting investors and what that might mean for KKR's businesses" [S393] REPORTED.

Block 5: the AI line

"Interns are encouraged to leverage KKR's approved AI tools to accelerate their work, deepen their learning, and contribute fresh perspectives on how emerging technology can enhance the way we operate" [Advert]. Three words matter. Approved: only tools the firm has cleared, because client and deal data are confidential. Accelerate: first drafts of research, summaries of long documents, formatting. Fresh perspectives: they want ideas from you on how the team could work better. KKR's London KCS analyst ad already asks for "Strong working knowledge of AI-enabled productivity tools, with the ability to use generative AI effectively and responsibly" [S140] CONFIRMED.

Say this in the interview

"I use AI for the first 70% of a task, like summarising a long report or drafting a structure, and then I check every number against the source. In a client team I would expect the approved tools to help most with first drafts of due diligence answers, which then need a human to verify." INFERRED

Block 7: eligibility, "Classification: Limited" and the SEO route

  • Eligibility. 2027 and 2028 graduates, undergraduate or Masters [Advert]. A 2028 graduate applying now is a penultimate-year student: this is a classic "summer before final year" internship that can convert to a graduate offer INFERRED.
  • PE off-cycle needs two internships. The Private Equity off-cycle seat asks for at least two prior internships, against one for everybody else [Advert]. If you have only one, ranking PE first is a risk, because you may not pass the filter for that seat INFERRED. KKR's live PE off-cycle posts in Frankfurt and Paris (minimum three months, 2027) confirm that PE uses longer off-cycle placements in Europe [S143] CONFIRMED.
  • "Classification: Limited". This is almost certainly an information-security label, the kind of marking firms put on documents to say who may see them, carried over from KKR's internal document system INFERRED. Do not over-read it as a statement about the role. Do take the hint: KKR labels information. Client Solutions handles confidential investor data and may be "wall-crossed" (given inside information) on capital markets deals, with strict information barriers [S70] INFERRED. Showing you respect confidentiality is a quiet plus.
  • SEO route. SEO London can help firms with shortlisting [S371] CONFIRMED, so SEO may screen your application before KKR sees it INFERRED. The AIP offers case study and modelling practice and "Interview guidance" [S372] CONFIRMED. Use it.
A smart observation to make

The Infrastructure paragraph says the team invests "out of a global $17bn fund" [Advert]. That matches the predecessor fund, Global Infrastructure Investors IV, which raised $17bn in March 2022 [S334] REPORTED. The successor, Global Infrastructure Investors V, closed at $19.2bn on 3 August 2026, KKR's largest infrastructure fund ever [S176] CONFIRMED. So the advert text is older than the latest fund. Saying "I noticed the advert mentions the $17bn fund, but Fund V has since closed at $19.2bn" shows you read primary sources, not just the job page. Say it as a helpful note, not a correction.

The Real Estate paragraph has a similar wrinkle. It says "As of Q4 2025, our team consists of 130+ dedicated investment and asset management professionals across 10 countries, with more than $85 billion" [Advert]. KKR's London Real Estate off-cycle post, updated October 2026, says "120+ ... across 11 countries" and about $84bn as of March 2026 [S142] CONFIRMED. Both are KKR's words; the numbers move with each update. Quote whichever you cite with its date.

2. The six teams, one by one@@m1-six@@

The six choices fall into two groups. Three teams invest: they decide what to buy (Private Equity with Global Impact, Real Estate, Infrastructure). Three teams make the investing possible: one raises and serves the money (KCS), one finances the deals and sells slices to co-investors (KCM), and one improves the companies after purchase (Capstone). KKR runs all of them as "one firm" with one profit and loss account and one compensation pool [S2, S5] CONFIRMED. That is why the links between them are real.

How big each team is in London

KKR's public people directory lists staff at Principal level and above (not analysts or associates). Counting London entries by team gives a fair picture of relative size [S149] CONFIRMED. KCS is the largest of the six intern teams in London at senior level.

The flagship funds behind the investing teams

Fund size tells you how much money each team has to invest and what KCS has had to raise. The chart below uses one consistent source: KKR's own fund table in its Q2 2026 10-Q, which shows each fund's commitments in US dollars at 30 June 2026 [S175] CONFIRMED. Commitments in the 10-Q can differ from headline closes because of currency conversion and KKR's own commitments INFERRED.

Source uncertain

Names and titles below come from kkr.com biographies read on 11 Oct 2026 [S149-S165] CONFIRMED. Bios can lag reality: one infrastructure partner is listed in London while moving to Milan. Reporting lines are never stated in bios, so any "who reports to whom" is INFERRED. Use names only if relevant, and only their public role.

2.1 Private Equity (including Global Impact)@@m1-pe@@

Private Equity buys large or controlling stakes in private companies with money from a fund plus borrowed money, works with management for roughly five years to make each company bigger and better, then sells. KKR's Private Equity business line managed $254.7bn at 30 June 2026 [S175] CONFIRMED, across 230+ portfolio companies [S191] CONFIRMED. In Europe, KKR said in 2023 it had been investing for "nearly 25 years" [S185] REPORTED. Global Impact is a separate private equity strategy inside this choice that backs companies solving big social and environmental problems while aiming for commercial returns [Advert].

KKR's own description (from the advert)

"A Private Equity Intern in our London office will be involved in various aspects of the private equity investment process, including sourcing and evaluating potential investments and presenting opportunities to the broader team, performing due diligence, and implementing improvements at portfolio companies. As we generally operate in small teams, interns will play an integral role and obtain significant responsibility from Day 1." [Advert]

PhraseWhat it means in practice
sourcing and evaluatingFinding companies that might be for sale, then a first screen: is the market growing, does it make cash, could KKR own it?
presenting opportunities to the broader teamWriting a short note or a few slides and defending it in a team meeting.
performing due diligenceChecking everything before buying: numbers, customers, market, management, legal risks. Much of it is coordinating outside advisers INFERRED.
Global Impact inside this choice

KKR's words: "a private equity strategy that scales companies providing commercial solutions to critical global challenges", focused on "climate action, lifelong learning, sustainable living and inclusive growth" [Advert]. Interns "support thesis development, industry research and sourcing" with "exposure to live deal diligence and portfolio company support" [Advert]. The tell is the last line: they want people "authentically passionate about impact investing" [Advert]. Expect to be asked which theme you care about, a company you would back, and how you would measure impact and returns at the same time INFERRED. London has 5 Principal-and-above Global Impact bios [S149] CONFIRMED; Rami Bibi is Head of Europe [S162] CONFIRMED. Global Impact Fund II has $2,709m of commitments [S175] CONFIRMED.

What an intern does

  • Financial analysis and modelling (the leveraged buyout model) [Advert]
  • Analyses that feed the invest or pass decision [Advert]
  • Due diligence and transaction execution [Advert]
  • Thematic and industry research [Advert]
  • Drafting IC memoranda for internal discussion [Advert]
  • Working alongside portfolio companies and operating partners [Advert]

Counterparties and tools

  • External: investment bankers and advisers (named in the advert), company management, lenders, co-investors [Advert] INFERRED
  • Internal: KCM for financing, Capstone for operations, KCS when a deal is shown to clients, sector colleagues across Europe INFERRED
  • Tools: Excel models, PowerPoint, IC memo drafts, KKR's approved AI tools for research [Advert]

What "good" looks like. A model that ties out with no errors, a clear one-line view on whether you would buy and why, and a memo section a partner can use with few edits. The best interns bring an idea nobody asked for: a company to look at, or a risk nobody spotted INFERRED.

How it links to KCS

KCS raises every European Fund. A successor fundraise is the obvious next big KCS project in Europe INFERRED.

Who fits. People who enjoy numbers and judgement in equal measure, who can sit with a model for hours and then argue a view in two sentences. For the off-cycle seat you need two prior internships [Advert].

2.2 Real Estate@@m1-re@@

Real Estate buys, improves and sells property, and lends money secured on property. In Europe that means warehouses (logistics), homes for rent, student housing and hotels on the equity side, and loans to property buyers on the credit side [S184] CONFIRMED. KKR first did real estate deals through private equity in 1981 and built a dedicated platform in 2011 [Advert].

KKR's own description (from the advert)

"Real Estate has been a part of the firm's strategy since 1981 ... In 2011, we decided to form a dedicated real estate platform. As of Q4 2025, our team consists of 130+ dedicated investment and asset management professionals across 10 countries, with more than $85 billion of assets under management. The Real Estate team is looking for motivated Interns to join the investment team in London." [Advert]

PhraseWhat it means in practice
investment and asset management professionalsTwo jobs: investment people buy and sell; asset managers run the buildings in between (leases, refurbishments, tenants) INFERRED.
$85 billion of assets under managementEquity plus credit. A later KKR post says about $84bn as of March 2026 and 120+ people across 11 countries [S142] CONFIRMED.
join the investment team in LondonYou sit with the deal team, not the property managers.

What an intern does

  • Underwriting models for acquisitions: rents, occupancy, capital spending, exit value INFERRED
  • Market research on a city or a sector (for example UK logistics) INFERRED
  • Due diligence with brokers, surveyors and lawyers INFERRED
  • Investment committee materials INFERRED
  • The London off-cycle post demands "Strong financial modelling skills" and "Demonstrable interest in Real Estate" [S391] CONFIRMED

Counterparties and tools

  • External: brokers, banks, sellers such as PLP, Ares funds and Curlew, partners such as Realty Income and Puma Property Finance [S184] CONFIRMED
  • Internal: KCS's European RE product team, KCM, asset management colleagues [S150] CONFIRMED
  • Tools: cash-flow models in Excel, PowerPoint, approved AI tools [Advert] INFERRED

What "good" looks like. Clean, well-labelled underwriting, a view on rents and yields that you can defend, and local knowledge (one market you know cold). For the German-focused off-cycle seat, German language is a hard requirement [S142] CONFIRMED.

2.3 Infrastructure@@m1-infra@@

Infrastructure owns the physical systems an economy runs on and earns steady, often contracted, cash from them: wind farms, fibre networks, data centres, rail fleets. KKR launched the platform in 2008 [S192] CONFIRMED. It now manages about $120bn of infrastructure equity, up from $13bn in 2019, with about 160 dedicated infrastructure executives [S334] CONFIRMED. In August 2026 it closed its largest infrastructure fund ever, Global Infrastructure Investors V, at $19.2bn [S176] CONFIRMED.

KKR's own description (from the advert)

"KKR's Infrastructure private equity group invests in companies with tangible assets centred around the key investment themes of energy transition, digitisation and industrial infrastructure out of a global $17bn fund and an open-ended core infrastructure strategy as well as a newly launched Climate strategy. Summer interns will be stepping into the shoes of a full time analyst, performing financial analysis, due diligence, industry research, as well as attending meetings with advisers and industry teams." [Advert]

PhraseWhat it means in practice
energy transition, digitisation and industrial infrastructureWind and solar; fibre, towers and data centres; transport and industrial assets. All three show in 2025-2026 European deals [S180, S181, S182] CONFIRMED.
a global $17bn fundThe predecessor GII IV. Fund V has since closed at $19.2bn [S176] CONFIRMED. Use this as your smart observation.
open-ended core infrastructure strategyDiversified Core Infrastructure Fund: no end date, lower risk, steadier yield. $14,855m of commitments [S175] CONFIRMED.

What an intern does

  • Financial analysis [Advert]
  • Due diligence [Advert]
  • Industry research (for example offshore wind or data centre power demand) [Advert] INFERRED
  • Meetings with advisers and industry teams [Advert]

Counterparties and tools

  • External: energy and telecoms companies as sellers or partners (RWE, TotalEnergies), co-investors such as Oak Hill, technical advisers, lenders [S180, S181, S182] CONFIRMED
  • Internal: KCS infra product team, KCM, Global Atlantic (an insurance account managed by KKR funded the TotalEnergies deal) [S180] CONFIRMED
  • Tools: long-dated cash-flow models, PowerPoint, approved AI tools INFERRED

What "good" looks like. A model that handles 20-plus years of cash flows, contracts and inflation sensibly, and research that explains a policy or market change in one page (for example how UK Contracts for Difference work) INFERRED.

2.4 KKR Capital Markets (ECM, DCM, Co-Investments and Partnerships)@@m1-kcm@@

KKR Capital Markets (KCM) is KKR's in-house investment bank. When a KKR fund buys a company, KCM arranges and can underwrite the loans and bonds. When a portfolio company wants to refinance or list on a stock exchange, KCM advises. And it sells slices of KKR deals to co-investors, including KCS's clients [S70, S174] CONFIRMED. KCM has arranged $2.65 trillion of financing since 2007 [S87] CONFIRMED. Capital markets transaction fees were $930m in 2025 [S70] CONFIRMED; in Q2 2026 about 85% were debt-focused and about 70% originated in North America [S1] CONFIRMED.

KKR's own description (from the advert)

"KKR Capital Markets (KCM) supports our firm, portfolio companies, and clients by providing tailored capital markets advice and developing and implementing capital solutions for investments and companies seeking financing. The Equity and Debt Capital Markets teams ... assist our portfolio companies with financing and capital structure improvement ... The Co-Investments & Partnerships Team within KCM works directly with KKR's investing teams across the firm's geographies and strategies to raise capital, structure, and execute transactions for the firm." [Advert]

PhraseWhat it means in practice
Equity Capital Markets (ECM)Selling shares: IPOs (first listings), follow-on share sales, private equity raises. Federica Gironi's bio lists the IPOs of SMCP and Pets at Home [S163] CONFIRMED.
Debt Capital Markets (DCM)Raising loans and bonds; leveraged finance for buyouts; infrastructure debt [S163] CONFIRMED.
capital structure improvementChoosing the mix of debt and equity, and refinancing when rates or performance change.

What an intern does

  • Analysis of debt capacity and capital structure options [Advert] INFERRED
  • Financing materials for lenders and investors INFERRED
  • Market updates on loan, bond and equity conditions INFERRED
  • Co-investment process support with investing teams [Advert]

Counterparties and tools

  • External: bank lending syndicates, bond and loan investors, co-investors, portfolio company finance teams [S70] INFERRED
  • Internal: every investing team; KCS for client demand; Global Atlantic as a co-investor [S70] CONFIRMED
  • Tools: capital structure models, market data, term sheets, approved AI tools INFERRED

What "good" looks like. Knowing what the market will bear today (pricing, terms, appetite) and turning it into a clear recommendation for a deal team INFERRED.

2.5 Global Client Solutions (KCS)@@m1-kcs@@

KCS is KKR's fundraising, client-coverage and product team. It finds investors, explains KKR's products, answers their due diligence, gets them into funds, reports to them for a decade and offers them the next product. KKR calls it "KKR's dedicated investor solutions team", formed in 2009, with "over 300 executives located in over 20 [offices] across four continents" [S141] CONFIRMED. KKR raised $305bn from the start of 2024 to 30 June 2026, beating a $300bn three-year target in two and a half years [S3] CONFIRMED. The deep dive is in the separate KCS pack; this profile shows where KCS sits among the six.

KKR's own description (from the advert)

"KKR's Global Client Solutions ("KCS") consists of experienced professionals with diverse backgrounds dedicated to developing and servicing KKR's global network of investors and clients ... Primary Activities: Facilitate client access to products and services across KKR's platform; Apply integrated approach by leveraging all KKR executives and capabilities globally; Work in partnership with Capital Markets in the syndication/distribution of product." [Advert]

PhraseWhat it means in practice
Relationship managers in direct outreach to clientsEach senior person owns a region or channel: UK, DACH, France and Southern Europe, Nordics, Middle East [S150-S155] CONFIRMED.
Product specialistsExperts by asset class (PE, infrastructure, real estate, credit) who own the materials and lead investor diligence [S106] CONFIRMED.
Junior resources serving in a generalist capacityThat is you: supporting several relationship managers and products at once [S140] CONFIRMED.

What an intern does

  • Support relationship managers on ad-hoc client requests [S141] CONFIRMED
  • Coordinate responses to due diligence requests and RFPs, including portfolio statistics and decks [S141] CONFIRMED
  • Prepare client briefing materials; support roadshow and AGM planning [S389] CONFIRMED
  • Maintain CRM data, market and client research, pipeline and budget tracking [S389, S141] CONFIRMED
  • Help with investor reporting, KYC and onboarding (London analyst duties) [S140] CONFIRMED

Counterparties and tools

  • External: pension CIOs, sovereign wealth fund teams, insurers, family offices, private banks and wealth platforms, investment consultants [S81, S150] CONFIRMED
  • Internal: product teams, investment teams, operations, finance, legal, compliance, risk [S140] CONFIRMED
  • Tools: Salesforce CRM [S103]; PowerPoint and Excel ("technical and aesthetic mastery"); AI productivity tools [S140] CONFIRMED

What "good" looks like. Every number in a client deck checked, briefing notes that make the relationship manager look prepared, fast and accurate answers to client questions, and a voice that can explain a fund simply to different audiences [S388] CONFIRMED INFERRED.

2.6 KKR Capstone@@m1-capstone@@

Capstone is KKR's in-house team of operating experts. Its people work inside the companies KKR owns to make them run better: pricing, purchasing, operations, growth. KKR's 10-K describes "operational guidance from our operating professionals at KKR Capstone" [S174] CONFIRMED. KKR counts about 980 "asset management professionals including those in investments, capital markets, and KKR Capstone operating roles" [S174] CONFIRMED. In London, Capstone is as big as the core PE team at senior level: 15 Principal-and-above bios each [S149] CONFIRMED.

KKR's own description (from the advert)

"KKR Capstone provides a unique opportunity for high-performing candidates to drive real operating change and value generation in a private equity environment ... KKR Capstone executives interact with a broad range of company personnel including the Board, C-suite and line-level operators. The majority of KKR Capstone team members have previous experience in management consulting ... they spend the bulk of their time identifying, rapidly prototyping, and executing operational improvement initiatives (i.e. less time spent on PowerPoint and more time dealing with general management challenges)." [Advert]

PhraseWhat it means in practice
drive real operating change and value generationMaking EBITDA (operating profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) grow through real changes, not financial engineering.
Board, C-suite and line-level operatorsFrom directors to the warehouse floor. You must talk credibly to all of them.
majority ... management consultingMost staff are ex-consultants. Juan de Ochoa, co-head in EMEA, joined from AlixPartners [S161] CONFIRMED.

What an intern does

  • Cutting raw company data to find where money is lost or made [S406] REPORTED
  • Benchmarking costs, prices or productivity INFERRED
  • Tracking improvement initiatives against targets INFERRED
  • Time with company managers, possibly on site [Advert] INFERRED

Counterparties and tools

  • External: portfolio company boards, executives and line operators [Advert]
  • Internal: PE and infrastructure deal teams; portfolio management committees (de Ochoa sits on the EMEA one) [S161] CONFIRMED
  • Tools: Excel and data tools, operating dashboards, approved AI tools INFERRED

What "good" looks like. Finding one number that matters in messy data, explaining it to a factory manager and a CFO in the same afternoon, and making a change stick INFERRED.

How it links to KCS

The link is real but less documented. KCS's job is to explain how KKR creates value; Capstone is one of the value-creation resources KKR presents to investors in its 10-K [S174] CONFIRMED. Capstone case studies in fundraising decks are an inference: no public deck was found INFERRED.

Who fits. Ex-consultant types, or students who love operations, data and getting things done. If your first choice is KCS, Capstone tests different muscles (structured problem-solving, mental maths) [S405] REPORTED.

Interview style hint. Reports describe three 30-minute interviews: CV and behavioural first, then a high-level case with simple mental maths on improving a metric [S405] REPORTED (anecdote); another mentions an analytical test "cutting raw data rather than building a financial model" [S406] REPORTED (anecdote). See Part 9.

3. The master link map: how the six teams connect@@m1-map@@

Read the map top to bottom. Money comes in from clients at the top, through KCS, into the investing teams' funds. Deals need financing (KCM) and improvement (Capstone). Companies are eventually sold, and the cash flows back up the left-hand side to clients, who decide whether to commit to the next fund. Every arrow is numbered; the legend says what moves along it.

The five links that matter most, with evidence

LinkWhat actually happensEvidence
KCS raises the money for PE, Infrastructure, Real Estate and Impact fundsEvery fund in the fund chart in Section 2 was sold to clients by KCS relationship managers and product specialists. The GII V investor list ("pension plans, sovereign wealth funds, insurance companies, asset managers, private wealth platforms, and family offices") is the KCS channel map[S141] [S176] CONFIRMED
KCM finances deals and syndicates co-investment to KCS clientsKCM "underwrites credit facilities and arranges loan syndications" and provides "syndication services for co-investments". If KKR cannot syndicate, it may have to fund the rest itself, so finding the right clients fast matters[S70] CONFIRMED; KCS works "in partnership with Capital Markets in the syndication/distribution of product" [Advert]

Key terms in the map

Co-investment: a client puts extra money directly into one specific deal next to the KKR fund, usually with lower or no fees [S84] CONFIRMED. Syndication: KKR or KCM commits to more of a deal than it needs, then sells the excess to others [S70] CONFIRMED. Re-up: an existing investor commits to the successor fund. Sidecar: a vehicle that raises outside money to invest alongside Global Atlantic through reinsurance [S70] CONFIRMED. DDQ / RFP: long questionnaires investors send before committing; KKR's CAPS team helps answer them [S146] CONFIRMED.

The life of one deal across all six teams

To make the map concrete, follow one illustrative deal: KKR's infrastructure team buys a stake in a European renewables portfolio. It is modelled loosely on two real 2026 deals, the 50% stake in a TotalEnergies renewables portfolio (EUR 1.8bn enterprise value, funded by an insurance account managed by KKR) [S180] CONFIRMED and the RWE offshore wind joint venture [S181] CONFIRMED. The steps and who touches them are INFERRED from how the teams are described in KKR's own texts.

Two things to notice. First, KCS appears at both ends: it raised the fund before step 1, and it owns steps 10 and 11. A KCS analyst is the person who turns an exit into a client update and a reason to re-up INFERRED. Second, step 5 is the busiest: KCM, KCS, the deal team, Global Atlantic and clients all meet at the co-investment. That is the exact point the official KCS description names: "Work in partnership with Capital Markets in the syndication/distribution of product" [Advert].

Say this in the interview

"What attracts me to KCS is that it is the team at both ends of a deal. It raised the money before the deal started, and it explains the result to clients at the end. In between, it works with Capital Markets to offer co-investment. In Europe that link is so close that the same partner, Mark Danzey, leads both Capital Markets and institutional client solutions."

Headcount estimate, with the method shown

The directory counts senior people only. To estimate the whole team, scale up using KKR's own total. Step 1: 232 KCS people at Principal level and above are listed worldwide, 46 of them in EMEA (47 with Mark Danzey, who is listed under Capital Markets) [S149] CONFIRMED. Step 2: KKR's Frankfurt posting says KCS has "over 300 executives" [S141] CONFIRMED; a February 2026 posting said about 320 [S106] REPORTED. Step 3: EMEA's 20% share of 300+ gives about 60. Allowing for a higher junior ratio (London is hiring analysts [S140]) gives a range.

Estimate: about 55 to 90 KCS people in EMEA, central estimate about 65, of whom about 25 to 35 are in London, as of October 2026 INFERRED. No reliable public benchmark for peers' London investor-relations teams was found. An internal comparison helps: KCS has 20 of 155 listed London senior people (13%), the same as London Credit and more than the London core PE team (15) [S149] INFERRED.

How big is the London office?

Companies House accounts give hard numbers for two London entities. Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co. Partners LLP, at 18 Hanover Square, averaged 182 employees in 2025 (97 "Executives and Associates", 85 "Administration"), up from 169, plus 88 members (partners), including 2 corporate members [S171] CONFIRMED. KKR Capital Markets Partners LLP averaged 10 employees and 10 members [S172] CONFIRMED.

So: about 286 people are counted in the two LLPs, and the best estimate for the whole London office is about 300 to 400 people (est., 2025-2026) INFERRED. Two numbers from these accounts are worth remembering. The main LLP is paid on a cost-plus basis for "sub-advisory services" to KKR's US adviser, so its turnover (GBP 177.5m) reflects costs, not the value of London deals [S25] CONFIRMED. The tiny KCM LLP made GBP 244.2m profit before members' remuneration in 2025, with 20 people [S172] CONFIRMED: capital markets work is highly profitable per head INFERRED.

@@m2@@
Part 2

The firm as a business, from the inside

Founding insight, the money flow, the contracts, the risk architecture, the centre, recent moves and the skeletons.

A. The founding insight: three people, a borrowed-money idea, and a firm built around it@@f-founding@@

KKR began as an idea that a big Wall Street bank refused to back. Almost everything about how KKR is built today (who owns it, how people are paid, how long client money is locked in) traces back to that idea and to the partnership of the three men who had it.

Bear Stearns and the "bootstrap" deals

Jerome Kohlberg Jr. ran corporate finance at the investment bank Bear, Stearns & Co. His two protégés were first cousins: Henry Kravis and George Roberts [S27, S28] CONFIRMED. From the mid 1960s the three did what they called "bootstrap" acquisitions. They bought mostly family-owned companies using a small slice of their own money (equity) and a lot of borrowed money (debt) [S27, S28] CONFIRMED. A reference history credits Kohlberg with first using the technique in 1965 [S27] REPORTED.

Key term

Leveraged buyout (LBO): buying a company mainly with borrowed money, where the debt is repaid from the company's own cash flows. The buyer improves the business, pays down the debt, then sells. Because the buyer put in only a small amount of equity, a modest rise in the company's value can multiply that equity many times. The "bootstrap" deals were the first version of this [S27, S28] CONFIRMED. (Fees, carry and fund mechanics are in the basics section; this part only uses them.)

The early results were mixed, which is worth knowing. Roberts and Kravis completed 14 buyouts between 1969 and 1975 with what one history calls "generally mediocre results" [S27] REPORTED. Some were spectacular: investors in Vapor Corp. (1972, about $37m) got 12 times their stake back when it was sold in 1978, and a Rockwell division bought in 1975 returned 22 times in five years. Others failed: Cobblers Industries (1971) went bankrupt [S27, S28] REPORTED. When Bear Stearns leadership refused to set up an in-house buyout fund, the three left to do it themselves [S28] REPORTED.

1 May 1976: "3 guys and a broom"

In KKR's own words: "On May 1, 1976, Henry Kravis and George Roberts co-founded KKR alongside their mentor Jerome Kohlberg with $120,000, launching what we now know as the alternatives industry" [S13] CONFIRMED. KKR describes the early firm as "3 guys and a broom" [S14] CONFIRMED. Its first buyout as KKR was A.J. Industries in 1976 [S28] REPORTED.

The first fund still appears in KKR's 2025 annual report. The "1976 Fund" took $31m of commitments and returned $537m: a 35.5% net IRR (the yearly return to investors after fees) and 17.1 times the money invested [S2] CONFIRMED. That track record is the reason pension funds later trusted three people with billions.

$120,000
Starting capital, 1 May 1976 [S13]
17.1x
Money multiple on the 1976 Fund ($31m in, $537m out) [S2]
50 years
Anniversary celebrated 1 May 2026 [S5, S13]

Scale, fame and the first break-up

The firm grew fast. Houdaille Industries (1979, about $355m) was then the largest LBO ever and KKR's first buyout of a major public company. Beatrice (1986, about $6.2bn) was financed partly with $2.5bn of "junk bonds" (high-interest, lower-rated bonds) arranged by Drexel [S27] REPORTED. In 1987 Kohlberg resigned, uneasy that KKR's deal hunting "disturbingly echoed the tactics of corporate raiders". He later sued over his reduced ownership; the case settled on undisclosed terms [S27, S28] REPORTED. Kravis and Roberts then ran the firm together as co-CEOs from 1987 until October 2021 [S10, S28] CONFIRMED. RJR Nabisco (1988 to 1989) made KKR famous and is covered straight in section I.

Source uncertain

You may read elsewhere that Capstone (KKR's operations team) dates from 2000 and KKR Capital Markets from 2007. Those dates were not confirmed in the research behind this pack. If you want to use them, check KKR's own history page first (kkr.com/about/history) [S13]. Safer line: "KKR added credit, capital markets, infrastructure and insurance over the 2000s and 2010s, and by 2025 traditional private equity was under a quarter of its money" [S2] CONFIRMED.

How the founding idea shaped KKR's design

You can draw a straight line from the 1976 idea to today's structure. This is the kind of link interviewers remember, because it shows you understand why the firm looks the way it does, not just what it does.

Mission and culture in KKR's own words@@f-culture@@

Two stories carry the culture better than any slogan. First, Kravis says his "best deal" was a company that went bankrupt: Walter Industries, bought in 1987. KKR spent almost 17 years and settled for over $300m (against $117m of KKR equity) to get fund investors their money back plus a small profit [S384] CONFIRMED. Second, he describes reprimanding an employee who "retraded" a loan deal with a bank in KKR's favour, and apologising to the bank's chief executive [S384] CONFIRMED. Both are about keeping promises to the people who trust you with money, which is the whole job of a client team.

Say this in the interview

"What struck me in Henry Kravis's 2024 pieces on culture was the Walter Industries story: 17 years spent getting investors their money back from a bankruptcy. For a client team that is the culture in one example. The product is trust, and KKR treats a promise to an LP as something you keep even when the deal goes wrong." [S384]

Source uncertain: "industrialist vision"

The phrase "industrialist vision" appears in the SEO London listing for this internship. Our research did not find it in any KKR document we read: the 10-K, the earnings releases, or kkr.com's About and History pages [S2, S12, S13]. Do not quote it as KKR's own wording. If you want to use the idea, attribute it: "the SEO listing describes KKR's industrialist vision", and then anchor it to something KKR does say, such as "supporting growth in its portfolio companies" [S1] or its ownership-culture programme [S387].

Don't say this

"KKR is a private equity firm." KKR describes itself as a global investment firm with asset management, insurance and strategic holdings [S1, S12]. Traditional private equity was under 25% of its money at the end of 2025 [S2] CONFIRMED. Also avoid generic praise ("prestigious", "market leader"). Use a number or a quote instead.

B. How KKR makes money now@@f-money@@

KKR reports three businesses, which it calls its "Three Engines of Growth" [S12] CONFIRMED. Each earns money in a different way. If you can explain the three engines and the "earnings ladder" in two minutes, you will be ahead of most candidates.

The earnings ladder, one rung at a time

KKR's earnings release builds profit up in steps. Each step has a name that analysts and KKR's own managers use on calls. You do not need the accounting, only the logic.

  • Fee Related Earnings (FRE): management fees, plus transaction and monitoring fees, plus fee-related performance revenues, minus the pay and costs tied to them. The steady, recurring profit of the asset manager [S1, S5] CONFIRMED.
  • Total Operating Earnings (TOE): FRE plus Insurance Operating Earnings plus Strategic Holdings Operating Earnings. KKR calls this "the more durable and recurring portion" of earnings. Introduced in November 2023 [S1, S11] CONFIRMED.
  • Total Investing Earnings: net realised performance income (carry after the staff share) plus net realised investment income (gains on KKR's own money) [S1] CONFIRMED.
  • Adjusted Net Income (ANI): TOE plus Total Investing Earnings, minus interest and taxes. KKR's headline "bottom line" [S1] CONFIRMED.
Why this matters

Investors pay more for steady earnings than for lumpy ones. That is why KKR keeps moving revenue into the "recurring" boxes. Example: from Q2 2026, performance fees from its K-Series private equity fund for wealthy individuals moved from carried interest (where 70% to 80% goes to staff) into fee-related performance revenues (where 15% to 20% does). CFO Rob Lewin said this "structurally increases" earnings per share [S1, S3] CONFIRMED. For a client team, this is the link: every dollar KCS raises into a fee-paying fund lands in the most valuable box. At 30 Jun 2026, $72bn of committed money was not yet paying fees, at an average of about 90 basis points (0.90%) [S1, S3] CONFIRMED. Simple maths: that is roughly $650m of yearly fees waiting to switch on once the money is invested (estimate, as of Jun 2026) INFERRED.

Fee rates in one paragraph

Management fees vary by product. Private equity drawdown funds charge 1.0% to 2.0% of commitments while investing, then 0.75% to 1.50% of invested capital; infrastructure and real estate 0.75% to 1.50%; CLOs 0.4% to 0.5%; open-ended vehicles 0.50% to 1.25% [S2] CONFIRMED. Carry is typically 10% to 20% of fund profits after a 6% to 8% preferred return [S2] CONFIRMED. Management fees were $4.1bn in 2025 and $4.6bn over the 12 months to Q2 2026, up 26% year on year in Q2 [S1] CONFIRMED. Realised carry was $1.88bn in 2025; $10.2bn of carry was earned on paper but not yet realised at 30 June 2026 [S1, S2] CONFIRMED.

The numbers over time

Say this in the interview

"KKR is really three businesses: an asset manager that earns steady fees, an insurer that earns a spread, and its own long-term holdings. About 84% of segment earnings over the last twelve months were the recurring kind. For a client solutions team that matters, because the money you raise turns into management fees, which feed Fee Related Earnings, which is the part of KKR the market values most." [S1, S3]

C. The contracts: who gives what, and who gets what@@f-contracts@@

A firm like KKR is a bundle of agreements with four groups: the clients who lend it their money (LPs), the people who work there, the shareholders who own the listed company, and KKR's own balance sheet. The trick is that the same people often sit in several groups at once. Employees own about 30% of the shares [S2, S3] CONFIRMED. Clients are sometimes shareholders too.

What LPs give and get

The fund mechanics are in the basics section. Here is what is specific to KKR. Fund lives vary by strategy: infrastructure and real estate drawdown funds invest for up to six years and last 10 to 13 years; credit drawdown funds last 8 to 10 years (up to 12); core private equity vehicles can last up to 25 years; open-ended vehicles have no end date [S2] CONFIRMED. Real examples from the June 2026 fund table: North America Fund XIV ($21.9bn committed at that date, investing April 2025 to April 2031), Global Infrastructure Investors V ($18.6bn, July 2024 to July 2030), European Fund VI ($7.5bn, June 2022 to June 2028) [S1] CONFIRMED. Both flagships later closed larger: about $23bn for North America XIV in April 2026 and $19.2bn for Infrastructure V in August 2026 [S334, S335] CONFIRMED.

Key term

Clawback: if a manager takes carry early in a fund's life and the fund later does worse, the manager must hand that carry back. KKR did exactly this in Q4 2025 on Asian Fund II: $344m repaid, $207m net after amounts recovered from current and former employees [S2, S4] CONFIRMED. It is the contract working as designed, and a good example to show you understand alignment.

What employees give and get

KKR pays from one compensation pool across the firm. The 10-K says pay "is based on the performance of KKR as a whole, in addition to an individual's contributions", and that KKR generally does not pay people "based solely on an individual's accomplishments in relation to the profits and losses" of one business [S2] CONFIRMED. Kravis says KKR has always worked this way, "creating a system in which we all succeed and fail together", and that everyone got "phantom equity" from the start [S385] CONFIRMED.

Carried interest from all funds is allocated to one vehicle, KKR Associates Holdings L.P., "the carry pool" [S2] CONFIRMED. The pay mix is base salary, a possible cash bonus, discretionary equity and, for select employees, a carry pool allocation [S2] CONFIRMED. On 29 November 2023 KKR made pay "more success based": more from carry, less from fees [S11] CONFIRMED. Bloomberg reported the shift: the staff share of carry went from 60%-70% to 70%-80%, and the fee-related share from 20%-25% to 15%-20% [S30] REPORTED; the new ranges match KKR's own deck [S5] CONFIRMED.

Say this in the interview

"Because KKR pays from one pool and most pay comes from carry, a person in client solutions and a person on a deal team want the same thing: funds that make money for clients. That is what an LP wants to hear when they ask about alignment, and I think it is a real selling point for the KCS team." [S2, S5] INFERRED

KKR's balance sheet and its shareholders

KKR's own money is invested next to clients'. At 31 December 2025, KKR and its employees had about $30bn invested in or committed to KKR funds and companies [S12] CONFIRMED. KKR says these "GP commitments" are usually required by contract, and also show "conviction"; it adds that their size has fallen relative to fund sizes as funds grew [S2] CONFIRMED. Employees and others put $612m of their own cash into KKR vehicles in 2025, mostly without paying fees or carry [S2] CONFIRMED.

Shareholders own KKR & Co. Inc. They get a dividend that KKR says it has raised every year since becoming a corporation in 2018: $0.78 a year from Q1 2026 [S1, S4] CONFIRMED. Until the Sunset Date (see section G) they cannot elect directors [S2] CONFIRMED. 891.6m shares were outstanding on 24 Feb 2026 [S2] CONFIRMED.

D. The operating model: four layers and what flows between them@@f-model@@

The simplest way to picture KKR is as four stacked layers. Clients sit on top. The investments sit at the bottom. In between are the teams that bring money in and the teams that put it to work. The KCS team, the one you are applying to, sits in the second layer and touches every other layer.

Three flows matter most for a KCS candidate. First, KCS is a two-way channel. It takes products to clients and brings client demand back to the investment teams. The Frankfurt KCS intern advert says the team "seeks to 'connect the dots' across all businesses at KKR, from our Private Equity investing teams to Infrastructure, Real Estate, Credit, Capital Markets and Insurance-Funded Strategies" [S390] CONFIRMED. Second, KCS and KCM work together on co-investment and syndication, which is where much of KKR's remaining deal-fee income now comes from, because fund-related deal fees are credited to LPs [S2] CONFIRMED; the link is the author's INFERRED. Third, Global Atlantic is both an engine and a client: its assets are managed by KKR's credit teams, and KKR reports "Total Insurance Economics" of $2.0bn over the 12 months to Q2 2026, which adds those fees to the insurance earnings [S1] CONFIRMED.

Governance and risk: who says yes, who keeps watch@@f-governance@@

KKR runs risk through committees, not single decision-makers. The 10-K says: "Our investment committees, or similar committees, review and evaluate investment opportunities using frameworks that are designed to include qualitative and quantitative assessments of the key investment risks" [S2] CONFIRMED. Committees exist per strategy and region. In London, for example, Tara Davies sits on the Infrastructure Investment Committee and the Infrastructure Portfolio Management Committee, and Mattia Caprioli on the European Private Equity Investment Committee and European Portfolio Management Committee [S16, S17] CONFIRMED.

Why this matters

LPs ask about governance in their due diligence questionnaires. A KCS junior helps answer them. Knowing that decisions go through named committees, and that pay is set on the whole firm's results, lets you explain why one bad deal does not lead a team to take wild risks to catch up. Lewin's line from 30 July 2026 sums it up: "Relationships travel, ideas travel, lessons learned travel" [S3] CONFIRMED.

E. How the business mix has changed@@f-mix@@

The single most useful sentence about KKR's evolution is in its own 10-K: "As of December 31, 2010, our traditional Private Equity strategy represented over 70% of our total AUM. As of December 31, 2025, traditional Private Equity was less than 25% of our total AUM" [S2] CONFIRMED. Fees tell the same story. Real Assets management fees almost tripled between 2021 and 2025 and now nearly match private equity [S2] CONFIRMED.

On 30 July 2026 CFO Rob Lewin listed growth since the April 2024 Investor Day: private equity up about 45%, infrastructure doubled, credit up about 35%, Asia up over 35%, third-party insurance up over 50%, and wealth up about six times [S3] CONFIRMED. Wealth is the outlier: K-Series grew from $16bn at the end of 2024 to $42bn in June 2026 [S1, S5] CONFIRMED.

Your opinion goes here

A defensible view: "KKR is becoming less of a buyout firm and more of a capital solutions platform. Credit is its biggest line, insurance is a whole segment, and wealth grew about six times in two years. That makes the client solutions job more complex, because you are now matching dozens of products to very different clients." Then add your own angle: which of these shifts do you find most interesting, and why? [S2, S3] INFERRED

F. A public company: why that is a gift for your research@@f-public@@

KKR has traded on the New York Stock Exchange since July 2010 (ticker KKR), after first listing in Amsterdam in October 2009 [S5] CONFIRMED [S28] REPORTED. It became a corporation on 1 July 2018 and joined the S&P 500 on 24 June 2024 [S2, S31] CONFIRMED. Being listed means KKR must publish a lot about itself. Most private firms you could apply to publish almost nothing. Use this.

What you can read for free on ir.kkr.com or SEC EDGAR: the 10-K annual report (FY2025 filed 27 Feb 2026), with fee ranges, fund terms, risks, legal cases and the founding fund track records [S1, S2]; the quarterly 10-Q [S332]; the quarterly earnings release, with a fund-by-fund table of sizes, dates and returns (Q3 2026 due 9 Nov 2026) [S1, S333]; the earnings call, the source of most management quotes in this pack [S3]; 8-Ks for material events such as Arctos, shareholder votes and the DOJ settlement [S6, S7, S8, S349]; and proxy and Investor Day decks (last full Investor Day 10 Apr 2024) [S5, S9] CONFIRMED.

How to read KKR's earnings release in 10 minutes

Say this in the interview

"I read the Q2 2026 release. What stood out was that KKR raised $305bn since the start of 2024, beating its three-year $300bn target in two and a half years, and that management said it was the strongest monetisation quarter in its history. For a client team, both halves matter: new money in, and cash back to LPs, which is what earns the next commitment." [S1, S3, S330]

G. Leadership and the future@@f-leaders@@

Who runs KKR

RolePersonBackground (public, professional)
Co-Chief Executive OfficersJoseph (Joe) Bae and Scott NuttallBoth joined KKR in 1996; Co-Presidents and Co-COOs from July 2017; co-CEOs from 11 Oct 2021. Bae built KKR Asia and had led or served on all private markets investment committees. Nuttall built the listing, balance sheet, credit, capital markets, capital raising and insurance businesses [S10] CONFIRMED.
Co-Executive ChairmenHenry Kravis and George RobertsCo-founders; co-CEOs 1987 to 2021 [S2, S10] CONFIRMED.
Chief Financial OfficerRobert (Rob) LewinLeads the earnings calls with the co-CEOs [S2, S3] CONFIRMED.
Chief Administrative Officer; Chief Legal OfficerDane Holmes; Kathryn SudolHolmes is ex Goldman Sachs [S2] CONFIRMED.
Head of Global Client SolutionsEric Mogelof, Partner, New YorkJoined 2020 from PIMCO (17 years there); also oversees Global Marketing [S18] CONFIRMED. (The KCS section covers the team in depth.)

When the founders handed over, Bae and Nuttall said: "We have spent virtually our entire careers at KKR because Henry and George are visionaries who not only shaped the business world but created a really special firm" [S10] CONFIRMED. Note the pattern: KKR grows its leaders from inside and over decades.

Investor Day 2024: targets and progress

On 10 April 2024 KKR set public targets for 2026 and beyond [S9] CONFIRMED. By mid 2026 the fundraising and fee targets were met, while the targets that depend on selling assets were behind. On 30 July 2026 Lewin said of the $7 ANI target: "as it relates to $7, we had removed obviously, that formal guidance last quarter. I'd say, in many ways, it has provided a bit of a distraction" [S3] CONFIRMED. Earlier in 2026 management had stressed it needed a "conducive market environment" for exits and had "modestly less visibility" [S39, S40] REPORTED.

Your opinion goes here

A balanced line: "The $7 miss looks more like a timing story than a business story. The targets KKR controls, raising money and growing fees, were hit early. The miss is in realisations, which depend on markets. I would also note two real headwinds: more competition in insurance, where Lewin said KKR will allocate 'a little bit less capital', and the Asian Fund II clawback." [S1, S3, S4] INFERRED

The Sunset Date, explained simply

In October 2021, alongside the CEO succession, KKR signed a Reorganization Agreement [S2, S10] CONFIRMED. Its last step is the Sunset Date. In the 10-K's words: "On the 'Sunset Date' (which will occur no later than December 31, 2026), KKR will cancel the Series I preferred stock, establish voting rights for all common stock on a one vote per share basis, and acquire control of the carry pool" [S2] CONFIRMED. Today, ordinary shareholders cannot elect or remove directors: the holder of the Series I preferred share, KKR Management LLP (owned by senior employees including Kravis and Roberts), appoints them. KKR uses the NYSE "controlled company" exemptions [S2] CONFIRMED. On 29 May 2026 directors were again elected by KKR Management LLP [S352] CONFIRMED.

In April 2026 shareholders approved three charter changes to prepare: meetings only (no written consent), the board fills vacancies, and the board fixes its own size [S6] CONFIRMED. The fourth, removing the 90% supermajority, failed for lack of quorum at the reconvened meeting on 21 May 2026, even though 97.83% of votes cast were in favour [S7] CONFIRMED.

Say this in the interview

"By the end of 2026 KKR becomes a normal one-share-one-vote company. The founders' special control ends 50 years after they started the firm. I see it as the last step of a handover that began with the co-CEOs in 2021, and something an institutional client who is also a shareholder might well ask about." [S2, S10] INFERRED

What leadership says about the future

  • Four growth drivers (Lewin, 30 Jul 2026): a growing industry with megatrends (AI, digital and energy infrastructure, defence); Asia (about 60% of expected global GDP growth); retirement demand from ageing populations; and a model that grows earnings without big headcount growth [S3] CONFIRMED.
  • Market mood (Nuttall): "In our time here, I don't recall a period of time where the external perception is so disconnected from the operating fundamentals and how it feels inside the firm." And: "Our industry is increasingly K-shaped... We find ourselves on the happy part of the K" [S3] CONFIRMED.
  • Five worries answered (Nuttall): private credit anxiety (KKR expects a record third-party credit fundraising year); wealth redemptions (K-Series net inflows up 20%+ year to date); PE exits (record monetisation quarter); software and AI (about 6% of AUM); slowing fundraising (KKR expects a record year) [S3] CONFIRMED [S362] REPORTED.
  • Big goals: "Multiple paths to surpass $1 trillion of AUM in the next 5 years" and "Strong conviction we can double Global Atlantic AUM" [S5, S9] CONFIRMED (targets).
Author's inference from hiring and moves

Recent senior hires and launches point to five priorities INFERRED: (1) distribution and wealth: Capital Group partnership, Doha Bank MOU signed by David Petraeus, KKR Middle East chairman (21 Sep 2026), new Asia-Pacific client head Bhavit Patel (Jun 2026) and a KCS Principal hire in Hong Kong [S22, S358, S359, S367]; (2) AI and power infrastructure: Helix, led by former AWS CEO Adam Selipsky [S3]; (3) secondaries and "solutions": Arctos and KKR Solutions under Ian Charles [S38, S355]; (4) insurance and Asia know-how: former Manulife CEO Roy Gori as senior adviser [S3]; (5) European policy and plumbing: Philippe De Backer for European public affairs (London) and Andre Serpa as EMEA Head of Treasury [S41, S42]. Each of these creates new products for KCS to explain. Treat the pattern as your reading, not KKR's stated plan.

I. The skeletons, told straight@@f-skeletons@@

Every 50-year-old investment firm has deals that went wrong and fines it paid. Interviewers rarely raise them, but a client asks about them in due diligence, and knowing them calmly is a sign of maturity. Here they are, with the facts and KKR's response.

IssueWhat happenedKKR's response and status
RJR Nabisco (1988 to 1989)KKR won a bidding war at $109 a share against management's $112, because the board judged KKR's bid more certain. About $25bn of equity value, about $31bn with debt; the subject of "Barbarians at the Gate" [S27, S28] REPORTED. One history says Kravis "clearly overpaid". KKR's own 10-K shows the 1987 Fund behind it made 8.9% net IRR and 2.4x, against 34.4% gross IRR for the 1986 Fund [S2, S27] CONFIRMED.No new LBOs for about three years after 1989; remaining stake traded for Borden in 1995 [S27] REPORTED. Fame, weak returns.
TXU / Energy Future Holdings (2007 to 2014)With TPG and Goldman Sachs' PE arm, bought TXU for about $45bn, the largest LBO ever. A bet that gas prices would rise; they fell. Chapter 11 on 29 Apr 2014 with about $49.7bn of debt; equity largely wiped out [S28, S32] CONFIRMED.A lesson in leverage plus a commodity bet. Shows why KKR now stresses durable cash flows INFERRED.
Toys "R" Us (2005 to 2018)With Bain Capital and Vornado, bought for about $6.6bn. Bankrupt September 2017, liquidated 2018 [S28, S33] REPORTED.KKR and Bain each put $10m into a $20m fund for laid-off workers (Nov 2018), not legally required; advocates said about $75m was needed [S33] REPORTED.
SEC broken-deal expenses (29 Jun 2015)The SEC found KKR misallocated more than $17m of costs from deals that never happened to its flagship PE funds instead of sharing them with co-investors, including KKR executives. "The first SEC case to charge a private equity adviser with misallocating broken deal expenses" [S20] CONFIRMED.Paid nearly $30m (over $14m disgorgement, over $4.5m interest, $10m penalty) without admitting or denying. KKR said it related to "historical ... policies and not to any current practices" [S20] CONFIRMED [S45] REPORTED.
Kentucky pension suits (2017 to now)Claims over accounts run by Prisma Capital Partners, a former KKR subsidiary, for Kentucky Retirement Systems; Kravis and Roberts named personally. The 2017 case was dismissed for lack of standing (final Feb 2024). The Attorney General's 2020 action and member suits continue; the Kentucky Supreme Court took up jurisdiction and indemnity issues (briefs Sep 2025) [S2] CONFIRMED.Contesting. Outcome not known in our sources as of Oct 2026.
SEC off-channel messages (Jan 2025)One of 12 firms fined $63.1m in total for staff using unapproved messaging apps for business. KKR paid $11m [S29] REPORTED.Settled. An industry-wide sweep, not a KKR-only case.
Asian Fund II clawback (Q4 2025)The 2013 fund ($5.8bn) had paid carry it later had to give back. $344m repaid; $207m net after recovery from current and former staff. 2025 ANI was $4.87 a share, or $5.05 without it [S1, S2, S4] CONFIRMED.Paid. The LP contract worked as designed.
DOJ Hart-Scott-Rodino (2025 to 2026)The DOJ alleged KKR broke US pre-merger filing rules on at least 16 deals in 2021 and 2022: altered documents for 8, omitted documents for 10, no filing for 2. 26 Aug 2026: proposed $250m civil penalty, the largest ever for HSR [S2, S21] CONFIRMED.KKR first sued, calling the penalties unconstitutional; then settled. It said it "acted in good faith", that "We strongly disagree with the Antitrust Division's characterization", and that the penalty "will have no financial impact on the firm, our funds, or any of our investors and will be fully reimbursed by outside law firms". Court approval pending [S21, S349] CONFIRMED.

The pattern in KKR's responses INFERRED: settle without admitting fault (SEC 2015, SEC 2025, DOJ 2026); stress that the issue is historical and practices have changed; fight first where it sees a principle (the DOJ countersuit); and occasionally make voluntary gestures (the Toys "R" Us fund).

How to talk about this if asked

1. Acknowledge, briefly and with facts. "Yes, RJR is the deal that made KKR famous, but KKR's own filings show the fund behind it returned 8.9% a year, well below its other early funds."

2. Separate type from size. "The recent issues are process ones: a filing case settled for $250m that KKR says outside law firms will reimburse, and an industry-wide messaging fine. They are not about investor losses."

3. Show what changed. "Since 2014 KKR's funds credit 100% of fund-related deal fees to LPs, and in 2025 it repaid a clawback on Asian Fund II. That is the contract protecting clients."

4. Link to the job. "In client solutions you would point LPs to the approved public statement, never improvise, and make sure due diligence answers match the filings." [S2, S4, S349] INFERRED

Don't say this

"KKR was fined for fraud" (no: the DOJ case is about pre-merger filings, and KKR disputed it). "RJR was a great deal" (KKR's own numbers say otherwise). "Barbarians" as a joke about the firm. And do not volunteer the skeletons unprompted; answer calmly if asked [S2, S21] INFERRED.

What these numbers do and do not mean

They do mean: the London LLP is a substantial team (about 182 employees plus 88 members, so roughly 270 people in this one entity INFERRED), its costs are rising, and it is run as a sub-adviser to the US parent "in connection with a number of Private Markets funds" [S25] CONFIRMED.

They do not mean: that KKR's London business "earns £177m". Under cost-plus, revenue is set by the LLP's own costs plus a margin, not by the fees and carry that London deals generate, which are booked by the US adviser and the funds [S25] CONFIRMED; the interpretation is the author's INFERRED. Nor is this all of London: KKR Credit Advisors (EMEA) LLP and KKR Capital Markets Limited are separate entities whose accounts we did not read. Say this in the interview

@@m3@@
Part 3

Why KKR is built this way

The mechanism behind the "one firm" model, where teams actually work together, what clients buy and why, and how the non-investing centre is wired into the front line.

Earlier parts described what KKR owns and how money flows through it. This part asks why. Why one profit pool instead of separate businesses? Where does collaboration really happen, and where is it forbidden? Why do clients hand over money for ten years and pay fees on it? And how big is the part of KKR that does not invest?

One firm, one P&L, one comp pool: the theory and the cost@@m3-onefirm@@

Most large asset managers grew by adding businesses. Each business often keeps its own budget, its own team and its own bonus pool. KKR chose the opposite. Its annual report says operating expenses "are shared across a single expense pool given the collaborative nature of our five business lines" and that pay "is based on the performance of KKR as a whole, in addition to an individual's contributions" [S2] CONFIRMED. Its 2026 shareholder deck lists the culture as "One Firm", "One P&L and compensation pool", "Collaboration" and "Business building & innovation" [S5] CONFIRMED.

Key terms

P&L (profit and loss): a single set of accounts showing revenue and costs. "One P&L" means the firm does not keep separate profit scores for each business when deciding pay. Comp pool: the total money set aside for bonuses and carried interest. Carry pool: the vehicle that receives the share of fund profits paid to staff; at KKR, carry from all funds goes into one vehicle, KKR Associates Holdings [S2] CONFIRMED.

The theory in four steps

  1. Clients are consolidating. KKR's 10-K warns that big pensions and sovereign funds are "consolidating their capital with fewer alternative asset managers" and want separately managed accounts [S70] CONFIRMED. In H1 2026, funds targeting over $1bn took more than 80% of all private equity capital raised [S336] REPORTED. A client giving one firm five mandates wants one coherent relationship.
  2. Coherence needs aligned pay. If teams were paid separately, a relationship manager would push the product that pays their team. One pool removes that pull. CFO Robert Lewin: "Relationships travel, ideas travel, lessons learned travel." [S3] CONFIRMED
  3. Alignment lets the firm stay small. Lewin again: "Our culture creates much of our investing alpha, which is why we have built a business model that allows us to keep the firm small and maintain that competitive advantage." [S207] CONFIRMED
  4. Ownership locks it in. Employees own about 30% of KKR's shares, against about 2% average insider ownership in the S&P 500 [S3] CONFIRMED. Henry Kravis describes the result as "creating a system in which we all succeed and fail together" [S385] CONFIRMED.

The boundary: what is shared, and what never is@@m3-boundary@@

A firm that both advises on deals (KCM) and talks to investors all day (KCS) has to stop some information moving. Some of KCM's work touches public companies and public securities; information about an unannounced deal is "material non-public information" (MNPI), and using or passing it on can be insider dealing. So the one-firm model has a wall built into it. The detailed rules are covered in the regulation part of this pack; here is the shape.

Why this matters for KCS

The KCS line "work in partnership with Capital Markets in the syndication/distribution of product" sits right on this wall. A junior who forwards a deal teaser to the wrong client, or chats about a live deal on WhatsApp, breaks the model. Saying in an interview that you understand why the wall exists shows judgement. INFERRED

The case clients buy is: access to deals they cannot do themselves, a manager whose own money is at risk on the same terms, and a long record. The 10-K lists what fundraising competition turns on: "investment performance, investor liquidity and willingness to invest, investor reputation, including focus and alignment of interest, duration of relationships, quality of services, and pricing and fund terms, including fees" [S70] CONFIRMED. That is KCS's scorecard written by KKR itself. INFERRED

The counter-case, with numbers

What a sceptical client would say
  • Records are uneven. The 1987 Fund behind RJR Nabisco made 8.9% a year net, 2.4x, against 13.5x for the 1986 Fund [S2] CONFIRMED. CalPERS's Asian Fund II made 1.0%, 1.0x [S117] CONFIRMED.
  • Money is locked up. Infrastructure and real estate funds last 10 to 13 years; core PE vehicles up to 25 years [S2] CONFIRMED.
  • "Liquid" products can gate. In Q1 2026 investors asked to redeem 6.3% of K-FIT, KKR's retail credit fund, and got about 80% of what they asked for [S338] REPORTED. Across the industry, wealthy investors asked to pull $20.8bn from private credit funds in Q1 2026 and managers paid out "just over half" [S337] REPORTED.
  • Fees compound. A 1.25% yearly fee on an evergreen fund [S111] is several times what a public index fund costs; the 0.84% Capital Group KKR fund is cheaper but still not cheap. INFERRED
  • No sourced benchmark. The research found no like-for-like comparison of KKR fund returns against public markets. KKR's claim of 2,072% total shareholder return since listing [S5] REPORTED is about KKR's shares, not its clients' funds.
Say this in the interview

"Clients accept the lock-ups and fees because they get access, alignment and a long record. KKR has about $30 billion of its own and its people's money in its funds, and it passes deal fees back to fund investors. But the record is uneven. CalPERS's numbers show some KKR funds at 15% a year and Asian Fund II at about zero. I'd want to explain both honestly to a client."

The non-investing side: the centre and how it is wired in@@m3-centre@@

Most of KKR does not pick investments. The people who raise money, report to clients, check compliance, run finance and operations, and build products are the centre. At KKR the centre is not a back office in another building. Job postings show it working in three modes: embedded inside a business, connecting businesses, and running shared services for everyone.

Size of the centre against the firm

  • KCS has "~320 employees" (Feb 2026 posting) [S106] REPORTED; a Frankfurt posting says "over 300 executives located in over 20 [cities] across four continents" [S390] CONFIRMED. KKR's public directory lists 232 KCS staff at Principal level and above [S80] CONFIRMED.
  • That is about 12% of the 2,705 asset management staff, and about a third as many people as the roughly 980 investing, KCM and Capstone professionals [S70] CONFIRMED; ratios INFERRED.
  • Put another way: for every three front-line professionals there is about one person whose whole job is clients. INFERRED

Why this matters

Three firms are bigger than KKR. Two of them (Blackstone, Apollo) also raise far more money in a year. So "Why KKR?" cannot be answered with size. It has to be answered with structure: what KKR owns, how it pays its people, and how those pieces connect. INFERRED

The competitive map@@m4-map@@

Since about 2021 the industry has split three ways in how it gets "permanent" money that never has to be handed back: owning an insurer (Apollo, KKR), managing insurers' money under contract without owning them (Blackstone, Brookfield), and selling evergreen funds to wealthy individuals, where Blackstone is far ahead [S201, S214, S221, S236] INFERRED. The map below adds a second question: how many different engines does each firm run under one roof?

Size, fundraising and staffing@@m4-scale@@

Three readings. First, KKR is the third-largest fundraiser in 2025 but its $129bn was its own record, and it beat its $300bn three-year target in two and a half years ($305bn since January 2024) [S207] CONFIRMED. Second, its AUM per person looks low only because Global Atlantic's 1,491 insurance staff are in the count. Third, KKR's stated aim is to keep it that way: Lewin says KKR can grow "without requiring us to significantly increase our headcount or sacrifice our culture" [S207] CONFIRMED.

The industry from zero

By the end you should be able to draw, on a blank sheet, how money moves from a pension fund into a KKR fund, into companies and back again, who takes what along the way, and why the people who raise that money (KKR Global Client Solutions, "KCS") are having a busy 2026.

$796bn
KKR assets under management, 30 Jun 2026 [S330] CONFIRMED
