1. Investing, and what an "alternative" asset manager is@@b-what@@

Investing means handing over money today to get more back later. The person or institution with the money (a pension fund, an insurer, a wealthy family) usually does not pick the investments itself. It hires an asset manager and pays it a fee. The asset manager's product is a fund: a pot of money from many investors, run under one set of rules.

Key term

Traditional investments are listed shares (stocks), government and company bonds, and cash. You can buy and sell them every trading day at a public price INFERRED. Alternative investments are everything else that big investors buy: private equity, private credit, infrastructure, real estate, hedge funds and natural resources [S269] REPORTED. Their defining feature is that they are illiquid: you cannot sell them quickly at a known price. In return investors hope for an illiquidity premium, a higher return than public markets INFERRED.

Five kinds of firm get confused all the time. Here is the difference in one line each [Inferred, standard definitions]:

  • Traditional asset manager (BlackRock, Vanguard): mostly index funds and listed share and bond funds. Very low fees, huge scale, daily liquidity.
  • Hedge fund: trades mostly liquid securities, often with monthly or quarterly liquidity, and aims for returns that do not move with the market.
  • Investment bank: advises on deals (mergers, listings) and underwrites securities. Paid per transaction, not a long-term management fee. Banks are counterparties and lenders to the firms above.
  • Private equity firm: buys whole companies that are not on the stock market, improves them and sells them, using funds that last about ten years.
  • Alternative asset manager (KKR, Blackstone, Apollo, Carlyle, Ares, Brookfield, EQT): a private equity firm that grew into many strategies. Runs long-lived private funds, earns management fees plus a share of profits, and increasingly owns insurance companies and runs products for individuals.

KKR is the clearest example of that growth. At 31 December 2010 traditional private equity was over 70% of KKR's assets under management. At 30 June 2026 it was "less than 25%" [S332] CONFIRMED. Today KKR's $796bn splits into Credit and Liquid Strategies $331bn, Real Assets $211bn and Private Equity $255bn [S332] CONFIRMED.

Say this in the interview

"KKR started as a buyout firm but is now mostly a credit, infrastructure and insurance business. Private equity is less than a quarter of its assets. So KCS is not selling one product, it is selling a platform."

2. The GP / LP structure: who gives what, who gets what@@b-gplp@@

A private fund is usually set up as a limited partnership, a legal form with two kinds of partner INFERRED.

Key term

General partner (GP): the manager. KKR, Blackstone, Apollo and Carlyle act as GPs. The GP picks the investments, runs them and decides when to sell INFERRED. It also puts in some of its own money, the GP commitment, so it has "skin in the game" INFERRED.

Key term

Limited partners (LPs): the investors who supply most of the money. "Limited" because they cannot lose more than they put in and they do not run the fund INFERRED. Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments, family offices and wealthy individuals.

The contract between them is the limited partnership agreement (LPA). Individual LPs often negotiate extra terms in a side letter, for example a fee discount or extra reporting INFERRED. The LPs' trade body, ILPA (Institutional Limited Partners Association), lists three guiding principles: alignment of interest, governance and transparency [S317] CONFIRMED. Keep those three words in your head: they are what every LP is checking when it meets KCS.

PartyGivesGets
LPA commitment (a legal promise to pay up to a set amount when asked); cash when called; patience for about 10 yearsMost of the profits; access to deals it could not do alone; quarterly reports; a say on conflicts (through an advisory committee)
GPDeal-finding, management, operating help; its own GP commitment; a track recordA management fee every year; carried interest (a share of profits above a hurdle); the platform to raise the next fund

The next page draws the whole system on one sheet. Learn to sketch it from memory. It is the single most useful drawing for a fundraising interview.

3. The life of a closed-end (drawdown) fund@@b-life@@

Most KKR flagship funds are closed-end: investors join only during fundraising, then the door shuts and the fund runs for a fixed life. They are also called drawdown funds, because the GP "draws down" committed money in stages. Think of it as a ten-year journey in four stages [Inferred, standard model]:

  1. Fundraising and commitment. The GP markets the fund. LPs sign a commitment to give, say, $100m when asked. No cash moves yet. The fund holds a first close (the first date it accepts commitments and can start investing) and later a final close (the last day it accepts new investors) INFERRED.
  2. Investment period (roughly years 1 to 5). When the GP finds a deal it sends a capital call (also called a drawdown) asking each LP for its share. LPs must pay within days. Money promised but not yet called is dry powder or unfunded commitments INFERRED.
  3. Value creation and harvest (roughly years 4 to 10). The GP improves the companies, then sells them in an exit: a sale to another company, a sale to another fund, or a stock market listing (IPO) INFERRED.
  4. Distribution. Cash from exits goes back to LPs. The fund usually has a 10-year life, often with 1 to 2 years of extensions INFERRED.

A real example: in April 2026 KKR held the final close of North America Fund XIV at about $23bn, which KKR calls the largest private equity fund focused only on North America [S335] CONFIRMED. Its LPs included public and private pension plans, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments and foundations, private wealth platforms, family offices and wealthy individuals [S335] REPORTED. That list is the KCS client map.

The J-curve: why the early years look bad

Plot an LP's cumulative net cash flow (all cash received minus all cash paid in) over the fund's life. In the early years the LP pays capital calls and fees but gets little back, so the line falls. Once exits start, it climbs. The shape looks like a letter J INFERRED. The bottom of the J is where LPs feel the most strain, and it is why slow exits in 2022 to 2026 hurt so much.

Why this matters

Exits have been slow, so the J has been stuck near the bottom for many funds. PitchBook counts almost $5tn sitting in funds that are seven years old or older, 39% of total NAV, as of December 2025 [S260] REPORTED. Bain counts about 32,000 unsold portfolio companies worth about $3.8tn [S262, S326] CONFIRMED. LPs with no cash coming back have less to commit to the next fund. That is the KCS problem in one sentence.

4. Fees and the waterfall@@b-fees@@

The industry shorthand is "2 and 20". The real terms vary by fund, and large LPs often negotiate lower ones [Inferred, standard definitions].

Key terms

Management fee (the "2"): about 1.5% to 2% a year of committed capital during the investment period, often stepping down later to invested capital. Pays salaries and running costs INFERRED.

Carried interest or "carry" (the "20"): the GP's share of profits, typically 20% INFERRED.

Hurdle rate or preferred return: the minimum return LPs must earn before the GP gets any carry, commonly 8% a year INFERRED.

Catch-up: once the hurdle is cleared, the GP takes a large share of the next profits until it has "caught up" to 20% of total profit INFERRED.

Waterfall: the order in which cash is paid out. A European (whole-of-fund) waterfall pays carry only after LPs get all their money back plus the hurdle across the whole fund. An American (deal-by-deal) waterfall can pay carry deal by deal, which is better for the GP INFERRED. A clawback makes the GP repay carry if later losses mean it was overpaid; ILPA's Principles 2.0 (2011) added a clawback appendix [S317] CONFIRMED.

Worked example you can do on paper

All numbers are illustrative. A fund has $100m paid in by LPs. After exactly five years every investment has been sold for $200m in total. The terms: 8% preferred return (simple, not compounded, to keep the maths easy; real funds usually compound), 100% GP catch-up, 20% carry, European waterfall. Ignore fees inside the example.

StepRuleMathsTo LPsTo GPLeft in the pot
StartTotal exit proceeds$200m
1 Return of capitalLPs get their $100m back first100$100m0$100m
2 Preferred return8% a year for 5 years on $100m100 x 8% x 5 = 40$40m0$60m
3 Catch-upGP takes 100% until it has 20% of all profit paid so farC = 20% x (40 + C), so C = 100$10m$50m
4 SplitRemainder 80 / 2050 x 80% ; 50 x 20%$40m$10m0
Total$180m$20m

Check: total profit is $100m and the GP got $20m, exactly 20%. The LPs turned $100m into $180m, so their net multiple is 1.8x even though the fund's gross multiple was 2.0x. That gap (plus fees, which we ignored) is why LPs always ask whether a figure is gross or net.

Now add the management fee. At 2% a year on $100m of commitments for a five-year investment period, the GP would collect $10m of fees before any carry (illustrative). The fee is paid whether or not the fund makes money. Carry is paid only if it does. That is why LPs like a large GP commitment: if the GP has its own money in the fund, it suffers losses alongside them.

Don't say this

"KKR makes its money from carried interest." Carry matters, but the steady engine is fees. KKR's Fee Related Earnings were $1.2bn in Q2 2026 alone [S330] CONFIRMED, and its fee-paying AUM was $638bn [S330] CONFIRMED. Say: "Fees pay for the platform; carry rewards performance."

5. Performance metrics: IRR, MOIC, TVPI, DPI, RVPI, PME@@b-metrics@@

LPs judge a GP by its numbers. Six abbreviations do most of the work [Inferred, standard definitions]:

MetricPlain EnglishFormula
IRR internal rate of returnThe annualised return, taking timing into account. Returning money fast boosts IRR.The yearly rate that makes all cash in and out net to zero
MOIC multiple on invested capitalHow many times your money you got back. $1 in, $2.50 out = 2.5x.Total value / amount invested
TVPI total value to paid-inThe LP-level version of MOIC: cash already back plus what is still held.(Distributions + remaining value) / paid-in
DPI distributions to paid-inCash actually returned. "Real money."Distributions / paid-in
RVPI residual value to paid-inValue still sitting in the fund, on paper.Remaining value (NAV) / paid-in
PME public market equivalentDid the fund beat what the same cash flows would have earned in a stock index?Fund result compared with an index on matched cash flows

The one equation to remember is TVPI = DPI + RVPI. NAV (net asset value) is the GP's own estimate of what the unsold holdings are worth, updated quarterly.

Mini-example (illustrative numbers)

An LP has paid in $50m. By year 6 it has received $30m in cash and the holdings left are valued at $55m. DPI = 30 / 50 = 0.6x. RVPI = 55 / 50 = 1.1x. TVPI = 0.6 + 1.1 = 1.7x. The fund looks good on paper, but only 0.6x is cash in hand.

Why IRR is not enough. Fund A doubles money (2.0x) in 3 years: IRR is about 26% a year, since 2 to the power of one-third is about 1.26. Fund B doubles money in 8 years: IRR is about 9%, since 2 to the power of one-eighth is about 1.09. Same multiple, very different experience. Always quote a multiple and an IRR together.

Why DPI is the word of 2025-26

If exits are slow, a fund can show a fine TVPI while sending back little cash. LPs need cash to pay pensions and to fund new commitments, so they now ask about DPI first INFERRED. The evidence:

  • Bain: distributions as a share of NAV were about 14% in 2025, and below 15% for four years running [S262] CONFIRMED.
  • McKinsey's 2026 report (via a Dakota summary): distributions fell to 6% of AUM against a 2015 to 2019 average of 16% [S261] REPORTED.
  • Bain cites an ILPA survey in which 53% of LPs said undrawn commitments limit new private equity commitments, up 15 percentage points [S262] CONFIRMED.
Source uncertain

Bain's 2025 report described 2024 distributions as the lowest rate in over a decade (one reprint says 11%), which does not square neatly with "essentially flat at 14%" in the 2026 report [S271] REPORTED. Quote the provider with the number, and say "about".

KKR leans into this. Its co-CEOs called Q2 2026 KKR's "strongest monetization quarter ever" (monetisation means selling or part-selling investments and returning cash) [S330] CONFIRMED. In August 2026 Aon agreed to buy USI Insurance Services from KKR and co-investors for about $17bn including debt, reported at about 6x KKR's original equity [S354] REPORTED. Exits like that are the best fundraising argument there is.

Say this in the interview

"TVPI tells you what a fund might be worth. DPI tells you what an LP can actually spend. After four years of distributions under 15% of NAV, DPI is what gets a pension fund to re-up."

6. The asset classes KKR's internship teams invest in@@b-assets@@

Candidates for the London internship rank six teams: Private Equity (including Global Impact), Real Estate, Infrastructure, Capital Markets, Client Solutions and Capstone. KCS has to explain all of the investing strategies to clients. KCS itself says it "connect[s] the dots" across Private Equity, Infrastructure, Real Estate, Credit, Capital Markets and Insurance-Funded Strategies [S390] CONFIRMED.

Risk levels and the growth and impact rows are standard descriptions, not sourced data INFERRED. KKR-specific markers: Global Infrastructure Investors V closed at $19.2bn in August 2026, KKR's largest infrastructure fund [S334] CONFIRMED; KKR's alternative credit includes $91bn of asset-based finance and $48bn of corporate private credit, of which $39bn is direct lending [S332] CONFIRMED.

7. Who the LPs are, and what each one needs@@b-lps@@

KCS's clients are LPs. Each type has different liabilities (what it owes in future), a different horizon (how long it can wait), different liquidity needs (how fast it may need cash back) and a different ticket size (how much it commits per fund). The descriptions below are the standard picture INFERRED; the research found no 2026 breakdown of how much each type holds.

Key term

Defined benefit (DB) pension: the employer promises a set income in retirement (say, a share of final salary), so the fund has fixed long-term liabilities and the employer carries the investment risk. Defined contribution (DC) pension: the employer and worker pay into a personal pot; the retirement income depends on how the pot performs, so the saver carries the risk. DC funds need daily pricing and switching, which makes illiquid funds harder to hold INFERRED. UK change: 17 workplace pension providers, covering about 90% of active DC savers, pledged in the Mansion House Accord (13 May 2025) to put at least 10% of DC default funds in private markets by 2030, with at least 5% in the UK [S315] CONFIRMED.

  • Pensions are historically the largest LP group INFERRED. Many are now over-allocated: S&P Global found 174 of 298 pension funds analysed were over their private equity target in Q1 2025 [S324] REPORTED. In the UK, the Local Government Pension Scheme holds over £400bn across 86 funds and is consolidating into six pools [S347] REPORTED: fewer, bigger clients.
  • Insurers are growing fast as LPs because they want long-dated credit INFERRED. KKR owns one: Global Atlantic had $220bn of AUM at 30 June 2026 [S330] CONFIRMED.
  • Private wealth is the big gap. Bain estimates individuals hold about 50% of global AUM ($275tn to $295tn) but only 16% of AUM held by alternative funds [S293] REPORTED. PitchBook: "Growing inflows from retail investors are becoming the main source of new capital" [S260] CONFIRMED.
Source uncertain

No 2026 figure was found for the share of global private capital held by each LP type, and no sourced ticket sizes. Do not quote percentages for "pensions are X% of LPs".

8. Evergreen (semi-liquid) funds versus drawdown funds@@b-evergreen@@

A wealthy individual cannot easily handle ten years of unpredictable capital calls. So managers built a second kind of vehicle.

Key term

Evergreen or semi-liquid fund: a fund with no fixed end date. Investors subscribe (buy in) monthly at the latest NAV per share, and can ask to redeem (cash out), usually quarterly, up to a cap, often 5% of the fund per quarter [S278] REPORTED. When requests exceed the cap, a gate applies and requests are paid pro rata (everyone gets the same fraction). Examples: non-traded BDCs (US private credit vehicles), non-traded REITs, ELTIFs in Europe, LTAFs in the UK INFERRED.

Why this is the private wealth channel's vehicle

  • Size: semi-liquid evergreen vehicles hold about $500bn of industry AUM (Evercore) [S267] REPORTED. US evergreen PE AUM nearly doubled from $51.3bn (end-2024) to $99.3bn (Q1 2026), which "funnels more capital into the hands of the largest GPs with established wealth products" (PitchBook) [S260] REPORTED.
  • KKR's version is K-Series, its family of funds for wealthy individuals sold through banks and advisers. K-Series AUM was $42bn at 30 June 2026, up from $25bn a year earlier [S330, S332] CONFIRMED.
  • The stress test: in Q1 2026 wealthy investors asked to withdraw $20.8bn from private credit funds run by Apollo, Ares, Blackstone, Blue Owl, KKR and others; managers paid "just over half" of requests [S337] REPORTED. Blue Owl enforced a 5% quarterly cap on 2 April 2026 [S278] REPORTED. Blackstone's BCRED paid 100% of record requests of 7.9% of NAV [S278] REPORTED. KKR's K-FIT received requests for 6.3% of shares in Q1 and paid about 80% of them; in Q2 requests fell to 1.65% and were paid in full [S338] REPORTED.
  • Europe and the UK have their own wrappers: 189 new ELTIFs since start-2024 and about €34bn of ELTIF assets at end-2025 [S302] REPORTED; the UK LTAF was opened to retail investors from 3 July 2023 [S305] CONFIRMED.
Your opinion goes here

Was Q1 2026 a failure of semi-liquid funds, or proof that gates work as designed? One defensible line: "The gates did their job. The lesson for a client team is to set liquidity expectations when the fund is sold, not when the queue forms." Decide whether you agree and why.

9. Secondaries, continuation vehicles, co-investment, SMAs and the denominator effect@@b-liquidity@@

These five ideas all answer one LP question: "How do I get the exposure I want, on terms I like, without being stuck?"

Key term

LP-led secondary: an LP sells its stake in a fund to a specialist buyer, usually at a price near NAV, to get cash early INFERRED.

Key term

GP-led secondary / continuation vehicle (CV): the GP moves one or more prized assets from an old fund into a new vehicle. Old LPs can cash out or roll over; new investors come in INFERRED.

Bain found CV transaction value grew 62% in 2025, but CVs were still less than 10% of exit value [S262] CONFIRMED. Evercore calls secondaries' shift "from an episodic liquidity solution into a structural portfolio management channel" [S267] CONFIRMED. KKR bought Arctos Partners (closed 4 May 2026); its team now forms "KKR Solutions", which KKR says will house "a scaled multi-asset class secondaries business" [S330, S332] CONFIRMED [S355] REPORTED.

Key term

Co-investment: an LP invests directly in one deal alongside the fund, usually with no or low fees [S260] CONFIRMED. It lowers the LP's average fee and lets the GP do a bigger deal. PitchBook tracks $37.5bn of co-investment fundraising in the 12 months to June 2026 [S260] CONFIRMED.

Key term

Separately managed account (SMA): instead of joining a pooled fund, one large LP gets its own account run by the GP, with terms, strategy mix and reporting built for it INFERRED. This is what "customized products" in the KCS job description points at INFERRED.

The denominator effect

Pension funds set a target allocation, for example "15% in private equity". When listed markets fall fast (as in 2022), the value of the listed shares drops at once, but private holdings are revalued only quarterly and more slowly. Private assets become a bigger share of the total even though nothing was bought. The fund may then be "over-allocated" and stop making new commitments [S323] REPORTED.

This was not just a 2022 story. S&P Global found 174 of 298 pension funds analysed over-allocated to private equity in Q1 2025 [S324] REPORTED, and PitchBook says institutional allocations are "bumping up against risk limits" [S260] REPORTED. Secondaries are one way out: an over-allocated LP can sell stakes to get back under target.

10. How big the industry is, and the fundraising market today@@b-market@@

Source uncertain: read this before quoting any number

Every data provider (PitchBook, Preqin, Bain, McKinsey) defines "private markets" and "fundraising" differently. Some count venture capital, some do not; some count only closed-end funds. The totals do not add up to each other. Always quote the provider and the scope together. McKinsey's own reports could not be read in full; only summaries were used [S264] REPORTED.

$6.1tn → $16.7tn
Private capital AUM, 2016 to Dec 2025 (PitchBook) [S260] REPORTED
~$32tn
Alternatives AUM forecast for 2030 (Preqin, Oct 2025; wider scope incl. hedge funds) [S269] CONFIRMED
$2.35tn
PE dry powder, 25% of AUM, Q4 2025 (Preqin) [S266] REPORTED

The fundraising story, year by year

  • 2024: fundraising fell around 23% to 24% across private market asset classes; Bain blamed the "persistent liquidity situation" for LPs [S271] REPORTED. McKinsey called it the lowest level since 2016 [S264] REPORTED.
  • 2025: Bain counts about $1.3tn raised in total, about flat, with buyout down 16% to $395bn, a fourth straight annual decline; growth came from infrastructure and secondaries [S262] CONFIRMED. Preqin: PE excluding VC $660.7bn, down 9%, with funds closed down 26% to 1,205 [S265] CONFIRMED. Cambridge Associates: fundraising "troughed in 2025 at roughly one-third of 2021 levels" [S261] REPORTED.
  • 2026 to 30 June: PitchBook counts $658.1bn across 1,499 funds in H1, with the 12-month total down 12.7% and fund count down 37%; if the pace holds, 2026 is the fifth straight annual decline [S260] CONFIRMED. But for the biggest firms it is a rebound: average time to close fell to 15.7 months and 82% of PE funds closed at or above target, the highest in at least six years [S266] CONFIRMED. And 7,739 PE funds are on the road, the most in five years [S266] CONFIRMED. KKR raised $34bn in Q2 2026 and expects "a record fundraising year for the firm" [S330] CONFIRMED [S362] REPORTED.

More signs of the flight to scale: in PE, 77% of capital since 2024 went to funds over $1bn; only 36 first-time PE funds closed in H1 2026, raising $7.7bn [S260] CONFIRMED. The ten largest funds closed in Q2 2026 took 49% of the quarter's capital [S266] CONFIRMED. PitchBook reads this as allocators "gravitating toward GPs with established track records and broad market validation rather than expending the resources required to underwrite smaller, less-proven vehicles" [S260] CONFIRMED. Bain: "Investors more than ever are focused on funds that have a clear, repeatable, and easily explained strategy" [S262] CONFIRMED.

11. The structural forces reshaping the industry now@@b-forces@@

Six forces matter most for someone joining a fundraising team in 2027. The map below puts each one next to its best data point and what it means for KCS.

What sits behind each force

  • Wealth. Executive Order 14330 (7 August 2025) told the US Department of Labor to re-examine 401(k) guidance [S273] CONFIRMED; the DOL proposed a process-based safe harbour on 30 March 2026, with no final rule found as of 11 October 2026 [S272, S274] CONFIRMED. Around 30 September 2026 the SEC proposed widening the "accredited investor" test beyond income and wealth, adding an exam and professional routes such as the CFA charter [S275] REPORTED. Bain projects private wealth allocations to alternatives could grow from about $4tn (2022) to over $13tn by 2032 [S293] REPORTED. KKR and Capital Group announced plans in December 2025 that include a target-date fund for 401(k) plans [S363] REPORTED.
  • Insurance and credit. Large managers own or partner with life insurers (Apollo with Athene, KKR with Global Atlantic). The insurer collects premiums and invests them in long-dated private credit the manager originates [S285] REPORTED. Apollo argues private credit is a market "of over $40 trillion", mostly investment grade [S285] REPORTED; critics say "private credit" as most people mean it is about $1.7tn to $3tn [S286] REPORTED.
  • Credit stress. Tricolor filed for Chapter 7 on 10 September 2025 [S282] REPORTED; First Brands filed for Chapter 11 around 28 September 2025 with liabilities over $10bn [S283] REPORTED. Jamie Dimon: "when you see one cockroach, there are probably more" [S280] CONFIRMED. BlueBay's Mark Dowding called Tricolor "corporate fraud rather than an underlying symptom of credit market conditions" [S281] REPORTED. Contrast: closed-end private debt funds had a record 2025 net cash flow of $39.5bn, behaving "differently from evergreen vehicles" [S260] REPORTED.
  • AI. Meta and Blue Owl's Hyperion data-centre joint venture issued $27bn of bonds, described as the largest private credit deal ever [S289] REPORTED. Redemption requests at Blue Owl's BDCs were partly driven by AI disruption risk to software borrowers [S279] REPORTED.
  • Consolidation. BlackRock's GIP and HPS deals were "the two largest-ever acquisitions of alternative asset managers in less than a year" [S290] REPORTED. Morgan Stanley and Oliver Wyman forecast more than 1,500 asset manager M&A deals through 2029 [S291] REPORTED.

Where the industry goes in 3 to 5 years: four competing views

ViewWho argues itCore evidenceIf right, for KCS
1 Structural growth via wealth and insurance (bull)Preqin [S269]; Apollo [S285]; Bain [S293]$32tn alternatives AUM by 2030; credit a $40tn+ market; wealth allocations to $13tn by 2032; US and UK rules opening retirement moneyHuge new client base; KCS becomes part sales force, part educator INFERRED

Pick one view and one piece of evidence that would change your mind. 12. What this means for a fundraising role@@b-role@@

  • The market shrinks, the leaders grow. Buyout fundraising fell for a fourth straight year in 2025 and PitchBook sees 2026 as a fifth straight annual decline for private capital overall [S262, S260], yet KKR raised $133bn in 12 months [S330]. KCS is where share is won INFERRED.
  • DPI is the opening question. LPs short of distributions ask about cash returned before anything else. Exits like USI are the evidence KCS uses [S354] REPORTED.
  • Two client worlds. Institutions buy drawdown funds, SMAs and co-investments; individuals buy evergreen funds through banks and advisers. KCS covers both, with different languages for each [S388, S390] CONFIRMED.
  • Liquidity is now part of the pitch. Gates, pro-rating, secondaries and CVs are basic vocabulary after Q1 2026 [S337, S338] REPORTED.
  • Fewer, bigger buyers. UK LGPS pools and £25bn+ DC megafunds want customised, fee-efficient access [S346, S347], which is the "customized products" line in the KCS description INFERRED.
  • Platform, not product. KCS "connect[s] the dots" from PE to infrastructure, real estate, credit, capital markets and insurance [S390] CONFIRMED. Knowing all six asset classes in this part is the entry ticket.
  • Trust is the currency. KKR's own line: "People do business with people they like and trust" [S384] CONFIRMED. Every number you give a client must be one you can source.
Say this in the interview

"Industry fundraising has fallen for several years, but capital is concentrating in large platforms: funds over $1bn took 78% of the money in the first half of 2026. LPs are short of distributions, so the conversation now starts with DPI and liquidity. That makes Client Solutions more important, not less: the team has to explain everything from a drawdown buyout fund to a semi-liquid credit fund, to a pension and to a wealth adviser, in their own language."

Don't say this

"Private equity is booming and everyone wants in." It is wrong on the data (buyout fundraising fell for a fourth straight year in 2025 [S262]), it ignores the 2026 redemption queues, and it tells the interviewer you have read headlines, not numbers. Also avoid quoting one total for "the industry" without naming the provider and scope.

@@m6@@
Part 6

The role's own industry and its regulation

Fundraising, distribution and the rules around them: the highest-leverage technical ground for a client-facing intern.

Why the client function has its own industry@@r-why@@

Private markets firms do two jobs. They invest money, and they raise it. This part is about the second job: the people, steps and rules that sit between an investor's savings and a fund like KKR's. It is the ground a Global Client Solutions (KCS) intern stands on every day.

The basics section explained the fund itself: a general partner (GP, the manager) and limited partners (LPs, the investors) signing a limited partnership agreement (LPA). Here we look at how an LP is found, convinced and kept, and at the walls of regulation that decide what may be said, to whom, and where.

$1.3tn
Private capital raised in 2025, about flat on 2024 (Bain) [S262] CONFIRMED
78.2%
Share of capital going to funds above $1bn, H1 2026 (59.1% in 2021) [S260] CONFIRMED
7,739
Private equity funds on the road chasing LPs, Q2 2026 (Preqin) [S266] CONFIRMED

Read those three numbers together. The pot of money is not growing. More funds than at any time in five years are competing for it. And the biggest managers take a rising share. In a market like that, the quality of a firm's client team decides who wins INFERRED.

A short history of raising money@@r-history@@

1980s to 1990s: the address book. GPs raised money mostly through their partners' personal networks. A fund was a handful of relationships with pension funds and wealthy families INFERRED.

2000s to 2010s: the professional IR team. As funds grew to tens of billions and LPs multiplied, the large GPs built in-house investor relations (IR) or "client solutions" teams. These have relationship managers per region or client type, product specialists per strategy, and junior generalists INFERRED. KKR's own team, KCS, was "first formed in 2009" and now has "over 300 executives located in over 20 [cities] across four continents" [S390] CONFIRMED. It is organised around "Sales/Relationship Management and Product/Strategy Management" [S390] CONFIRMED.

2010s: the LP pushes back. LPs organised. The Institutional Limited Partners Association (ILPA) published its first Principles in September 2009 and its first due diligence questionnaire in 2013 [S317, S320] CONFIRMED. Fund terms, reporting and diligence became more standard.

2020s: the individual arrives. Bain estimates individuals hold about 50% of global assets ($275tn to $295tn) but only 16% of the assets held in alternative funds [S293] REPORTED. Closing that gap is the "democratisation" story. Platforms such as iCapital and CAIS, plus wirehouses and private banks, now carry private funds to wealthy individuals. PitchBook says "growing inflows from retail investors are becoming the main source of new capital" for private equity [S260] CONFIRMED.

Why this matters

KKR's 10-Q says traditional private equity was over 70% of its assets in 2010 and is "less than 25%" today [S332] CONFIRMED. The client function grew up alongside that shift: more products, more client types, more rules. A KCS junior now explains credit, infrastructure, insurance-backed strategies and wealth funds, not one buyout fund.

The players: who stands between savings and a fund@@r-players@@

The map below shows the cast. Two flows matter. Money moves along the solid lines. Advice, introductions, rules and standards move along the dashed lines. The GP's client team sits in the middle of both.

PlayerWhat they do, in plain EnglishExamples and facts
GP client teamFinds, wins and keeps investors. Answers every question after the money arrives.KKR KCS: relationship managers, product specialists, junior generalists (official team text). Works "in partnership with Capital Markets in the syndication/distribution of product".
Placement agentAn outside firm hired by a GP to raise money, often for mid-sized or first-time managers, or to reach new LP types.Evercore, Campbell Lutyens, Park Hill (PJT), Lazard, Rede, Asante. PEI's ranking to May 2024 covered 38 agents raising $41bn of "new" capital [S322] REPORTED. Typical success fee around 2% to 2.5% of capital raised (indicative only) [S322] REPORTED.
Investment consultant / gatekeeperAdvises an LP on which funds to back. Often the first screen a fund must pass.Cambridge Associates, Mercer, Aon, Hamilton Lane, StepStone (the last two also invest directly) INFERRED.
Feeder platformLets a wealth adviser put many clients into one "feeder" fund that invests in the GP's fund. Handles paperwork, minimums, reporting.iCapital (founded 2013) raised $820m in July 2025 at a reported $7.5bn valuation [S321] REPORTED. CAIS.
Wirehouse / private bankLarge brokerages and banks whose advisers sell funds to wealthy clients.Morgan Stanley, Merrill, UBS, Wells Fargo INFERRED.
ILPAThe LPs' trade body. Writes best-practice terms and standard templates.Offices in Toronto, Washington DC and London [S317] CONFIRMED.
Key terms

Gatekeeper: anyone who controls access to an LP's money, usually a consultant. Feeder fund: a small fund whose only job is to pool many investors and invest in one bigger fund. Re-up: an existing LP committing to the manager's next fund. Re-ups are the cheapest money a client team ever raises INFERRED.

How an institutional LP picks a manager@@r-funnel@@

A pension fund does not wire $200m after one good meeting. Selection takes months and passes through a funnel of checks (see the funnel figure). Each stage creates work for the GP's client team. The KKR EMEA client relations analyst advert lists exactly this work: "investor reporting", "supporting relationship managers in fundraising", "KYC and onboarding", and answering requests with product, investment, operations, finance, legal, compliance and risk teams [S388] CONFIRMED.

The stages in words

  1. Screening. The LP or its consultant filters by track record, strategy fit and team stability INFERRED.
  2. Investment due diligence. Deal-by-deal attribution (which deals made the money), DPI (cash actually returned divided by cash paid in), PME (a comparison with a stock index), and reference calls INFERRED.
  3. Due diligence questionnaire (DDQ). A long standard form, often the ILPA DDQ. The first ILPA DDQ came out in 2013, was updated in 2016 and 2018, and DDQ 2.0 arrived in November 2021 with new sections on succession planning, co-investment, GP-led secondaries, credit facilities and cybersecurity [S320] REPORTED.
  4. Operational due diligence (ODD). A separate team checks the back office: valuation policy, cyber, compliance, administrator, auditor. The FCA's March 2025 review of private market valuations found weaknesses in governance records, conflicts, independence and ad hoc revaluations [S310] REPORTED. Expect ODD teams to ask about exactly those.
  5. Investment committee. The LP's own board or committee approves INFERRED.
  6. Legal. LPA terms and a side letter: a private contract giving one LP extra terms such as fee breaks, reporting rights, co-investment rights or the right to skip certain deals. A most-favoured-nation (MFN) clause lets an LP claim terms given to similar or smaller LPs INFERRED.
  7. Commitment and monitoring. Quarterly reports, annual meetings, a seat on the LP advisory committee (LPAC) for big LPs, and in time the next re-up INFERRED.

ILPA: the rule book written by the clients@@r-ilpa@@

ILPA's three guiding principles are alignment of interest, governance and transparency, which it says "form the essence of an effective private equity partnership" [S317] CONFIRMED. ILPA has no legal power. Its weight comes from the fact that its members are the LPs.

  • Cash back (DPI). Exits have been slow, so LPs are short of distributions. This is the most-watched number in every meeting [S262] CONFIRMED.
  • A clear, repeatable strategy. Bain: "Investors more than ever are focused on funds that have a clear, repeatable, and easily explained strategy" [S262] CONFIRMED. This is a communication skill as much as an investment one.
  • Co-investment (investing directly next to the fund, usually at low or no fee) [S260] CONFIRMED.

Regulation in one picture: who may be marketed what@@r-map@@

All fundraising rules answer one question: who is this investor, and where are they? Professional investors are assumed to look after themselves. Ordinary savers are protected, so they can only buy private assets through special, regulated products. The map below is the one to carry into an interview.

The European Union@@r-eu@@

AIFMD: the base law

The Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive (AIFMD), Directive 2011/61/EU, regulates managers of "alternative" funds: private equity, credit, real estate and hedge funds. It was signed on 8 June 2011, entered into force on 21 July 2011 (some sources say 22 July), and had to be in national law by 22 July 2013 [S300] CONFIRMED.

  • Marketing passport. From 22 July 2013 an EU manager could sell an EU fund to professional investors across the EU after a notification [S300] CONFIRMED.
  • NPPR (national private placement regime). Non-EU managers have no passport. They use each country's own private placement rules under Article 42, country by country [S300] CONFIRMED.

Pre-marketing and reverse solicitation

The Cross-Border Distribution package (Directive (EU) 2019/1160 and Regulation (EU) 2019/1156) was published on 12 July 2019, came into force on 1 August 2019 and applied from 2 August 2021 [S299] CONFIRMED. It defined pre-marketing: testing investor interest before a fund is set up or notified, without an offer. An EU manager must tell its home regulator within two weeks of starting. AIMA's summary: "Within two weeks of starting to pre-market, an EU AIFM must send an informal letter or email to its home regulator" [S299] CONFIRMED.

Reverse solicitation means the investor approached the manager on its own initiative, so no "marketing" happened. The package closed the loophole: any subscription by a professional investor within 18 months of pre-marketing counts as marketing [S299] CONFIRMED. For a client team, this means every early conversation in Europe is logged and timed.

AIFMD II

Directive (EU) 2024/927 was published in the Official Journal on 26 March 2024, entered into force on 15 April 2024, and had to apply from 16 April 2026 [S296, S294] CONFIRMED. Linklaters marked the day: "AIFMD II takes effect at last" [S344] CONFIRMED.

ChangeDetailWhy a client team cares
Loan-originating fundsLeverage caps of 175% (open-ended) and 300% (closed-ended); 20% limit per financial borrower; keep 5% of each loan sold; no "originate-to-distribute"; closed-ended unless liquidity fits [S295, S297] CONFIRMEDShapes how European direct-lending funds are built and described
Liquidity management tools (LMTs)Open-ended funds must pick at least two from a list: gates, notice periods, redemption fees, swing pricing, and others [S295, S294] CONFIRMED. Commission adopted the LMT standards on 17 Nov 2025; ESMA guidelines published 12 Mar 2026 [S298] REPORTEDExplains to wealth clients why they cannot always exit when they want
DelegationMore reporting on delegation; at least two full-time EU-resident people running the business [S294] REPORTEDAffects where European fund entities sit
NPPR tighteningNon-EU managers and funds must not be in EU AML high-risk or tax non-cooperative lists [S294] REPORTEDFund domicile choice
GrandfatheringLoan funds set up before 15 Apr 2024 are exempt until 16 Apr 2029 [S297] CONFIRMEDOlder funds behave differently

Not every country was ready: Belgium, for example, had not published its law by the deadline [S294] REPORTED. New reporting starts on 16 April 2027, and the Commission said non-essential Level 2 detail would wait until after 1 October 2027 [S344, S298] CONFIRMED.

ELTIF 2.0 and MiFID II

The European Long-Term Investment Fund regulation, revised as Regulation (EU) 2023/606 ("ELTIF 2.0"), applies from 10 January 2024. It removed the €10,000 minimum for retail investors and widened eligible assets. Its technical standards became Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/2759, published on 25 October 2024 [S301, S302] CONFIRMED. Morningstar counts 189 new ELTIFs since the start of 2024; Scope counts a record 113 launches in 2025 and about €34bn of assets at end-2025, up 55% [S302] REPORTED.

MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU) has applied since 3 January 2018. Its product governance rules make manufacturers and distributors define a "target market" for each product, so a fund is only sold to the kind of client it was designed for INFERRED (dates not re-verified).

The United Kingdom@@r-uk@@

The UK AIFM regime and its rewrite

The UK put AIFMD into law in 2013 and kept it after Brexit. Overseas funds still reach UK investors through the UK NPPR [S304] REPORTED. HM Treasury and the FCA opened a reform consultation on 7 April 2025 [S304] CONFIRMED. Then came FCA CP26/28 "The UK AIFM Regime", published in July 2026 (14 July per Macfarlanes; Debevoise's note is dated 23 July) [S345, S303] CONFIRMED.

  • A new "ALTS" sourcebook. Investor disclosures become less prescriptive; firms choose how to disclose leverage [S303, S345] CONFIRMED.
  • UK managers marketing UK funds move from a 20-day pre-approval to a simple notification. NPPR kept with limited changes [S303] CONFIRMED.
  • Companion papers: CP26/27 on pay (the FCA "does not propose to make malus and clawback mandatory") and CP26/26 on reporting [S303] CONFIRMED.
  • Comments close on 14 October 2026, three days after this pack was written. Policy statement in 2027; rules in force 2028 [S303] CONFIRMED.

Retail and wealth routes in the UK

  • LTAF (Long-Term Asset Fund). Rules in force 15 November 2021. PS23/7 (29 June 2023) made LTAF units "Restricted Mass Market Investments" from 3 July 2023, opening them to retail investors with protections, and to self-select DC pensions and SIPPs [S305, S306] CONFIRMED.
  • Financial promotions exemptions. On 31 January 2024 the high-net-worth thresholds rose to £170,000 income or £430,000 net assets. After an industry backlash a new order from 27 March 2024 restored £100,000 and £250,000 and brought back the "two or more unlisted investments" test for self-certified sophisticated investors [S307] CONFIRMED. A good example of rules moving twice in two months.
  • Consumer Duty. Applied to open products from 31 July 2023 and closed products from 31 July 2024. It requires firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers [S308] CONFIRMED.
  • SMCR (Senior Managers and Certification Regime). Extended to FCA solo-regulated firms, which include most UK private markets managers, on 9 December 2019 (PS19/20) [S309] CONFIRMED. It makes named senior people personally accountable.

UK pensions: the Mansion House Accord and the Pension Schemes Act 2026

The Mansion House Accord (13 May 2025) is voluntary. 17 workplace pension providers, covering about 90% of active defined contribution (DC) savers, pledged to put at least 10% of DC default funds into private markets by 2030, with at least 5% in the UK. It could unlock up to £50bn, about £25bn in the UK [S315] CONFIRMED. HM Treasury: "At least 5 percent of these portfolios will be ringfenced for the UK" [S315] CONFIRMED.

The Pension Schemes Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 29 April 2026 after the Bill was introduced on 5 June 2025 [S316, S346] CONFIRMED. Main points:

  • Large multi-employer DC schemes need a default fund of at least £25bn by 2030 ("megafunds"); a transition route exists for schemes of £10bn or more that can reach £25bn by 2035 [S346] CONFIRMED.
  • A reserve power lets the government, once and not before 1 January 2028, require megafunds to hold "qualifying assets" (private equity, venture capital, private credit, land, infrastructure, unlisted shares). Cap: 10% of the default fund, of which no more than 5% UK-specific. Trustees can opt out if compliance is "likely not to be in the best interests of members". The power lapses at end-2032 if unused [S346] CONFIRMED.
  • Separately, the Local Government Pension Scheme (over £400bn across 86 funds in England and Wales) is consolidating from eight pools into six [S347] REPORTED.

The United States@@r-us@@

  • Regulation D. Rule 506(b) allows private offerings with no general solicitation (advertising). Rule 506(c), effective 23 September 2013 under the JOBS Act, allows general solicitation if every buyer is a verified accredited investor [S314] CONFIRMED.
  • Accredited investor. An individual with income over $200,000 ($300,000 joint) in each of the last two years, or net worth over $1m excluding the home [S314] CONFIRMED. August 2020 amendments added professional licence routes (Series 7, 65, 82) [S275] REPORTED. Around 30 September 2026 the SEC proposed a FINRA-developed accredited investor exam (pass valid ten years) plus Series 79, 86 and 87, CPA, CFA and CFP routes, with a 60-day comment period [S275] REPORTED. Chairman Paul Atkins: "accredited investor access to private offerings should not be limited solely to individuals satisfying financial thresholds" [S275] REPORTED.
  • Marketing Rule (Rule 206(4)-1). Adopted 22 December 2020, effective 4 May 2021, compliance from 4 November 2022. It replaced the old advertising and cash solicitation rules [S313] CONFIRMED. It governs how performance is shown in any pitch book.
  • Private Fund Adviser Rules. Adopted August 2023 (quarterly statements, audits, restricted activities, preferential treatment, adviser-led secondaries). Vacated in full by the Fifth Circuit on 5 June 2024 in National Association of Private Fund Managers v. SEC [S311, S312] CONFIRMED. Much of what they required now travels through ILPA templates and side letters instead INFERRED.
  • 401(k) access. Executive Order 14330, "Democratizing Access to Alternative Assets for 401(k) Investors", signed 7 August 2025 [S273] CONFIRMED. The Department of Labor proposed a process-based safe harbour on 30 March 2026, with six factors: performance, fees, liquidity, valuation, benchmarks and complexity. Comments closed 1 June 2026 [S272, S274, S342] CONFIRMED. No final rule found as of 11 October 2026 [S343] REPORTED.
  • SEC retail agenda. A roundtable on retail access to private investments on 4 March 2026 [S277] REPORTED; in early October 2026 the SEC reportedly voted to propose wider retail access through regulated funds [S368] REPORTED.

The regulation timeline, 2011 to 2028@@r-timeline@@

The walls around a client function@@r-walls@@

A client team talks to outsiders all day, and it sits inside a firm that holds secrets. Four kinds of wall keep the two apart (see the figure below). The detail differs by firm and is set by each firm's compliance team; what follows is the standard industry pattern, not KKR's internal policy INFERRED.

  • Information barrier (the "Chinese wall"). Separates people with MNPI from people who trade listed securities. Breaching it risks insider dealing INFERRED.
  • Need-to-know wall. A client team learns about live deals only when compliance approves it ("wall-crossing"). Example: before DCC confirmed an approach from Energy Capital Partners and KKR on 29 April 2026, any knowledge of the bid would have been MNPI about a London-listed company [S356] REPORTED. The application to KCS is INFERRED.
  • Marketing gate. Every pitch book, DDQ answer and performance figure is approved before it leaves. It must match the investor type and country (the "who may be marketed what" map), meet EU pre-marketing timing and the Marketing Rule in the US [S299, S313] CONFIRMED; how firms apply them is INFERRED.
  • Gifts and entertainment. Hospitality given or received is logged, kept within limits and pre-approved where policy requires; extra care applies to public pension officials INFERRED.
Why this matters

On governance, litigation and regulation, LP questionnaires want the approved answer. On the August 2026 DOJ settlement, KKR's public line is that the $250m civil penalty "will have no financial impact on the firm, our funds, or any of our investors and will be fully reimbursed by outside law firms" [S349] CONFIRMED. A junior repeats that line and nothing more.

What to say about all this@@r-say@@

What a candidate should be able to say unprompted

  1. "Fundraising is concentrating: funds above $1bn took 78.2% of capital in H1 2026, against 59.1% in 2021." [S260]
  2. "LPs choose through a funnel: consultant screen, due diligence, the ILPA DDQ, operational due diligence, investment committee, side letter, then commitment."
  3. "In Europe a non-EU manager markets through national private placement; AIFMD II applied from 16 April 2026." [S300, S294]
  4. "In the UK, CP26/28 proposes three tiers of manager by size, with new rules in 2028; the Pension Schemes Act 2026 caps any mandation at 10% private, 5% UK." [S303, S346]
  5. "In the US the direction is wider access: EO 14330 in August 2025, the DOL safe harbour proposal in March 2026, and the SEC's accredited investor proposal this autumn." [S273, S272, S275]
Say this in the interview

"Regulation is moving in two directions at once. Access is widening for individuals, through ELTIF 2.0, the LTAF and the US 401(k) work. But the rules on credit funds and liquidity are getting tighter, through AIFMD II. A client team has to sell the first while explaining the second."

Don't say this

"The Mansion House Accord forces UK pensions to invest 10% in private markets." It is voluntary. The legal backstop is a reserve power in the Pension Schemes Act 2026, capped at the same 10% / 5% levels and not usable before 1 January 2028 [S315, S346].

Say this in the interview

"The SEC's private fund adviser rules were vacated in June 2024, so a lot of LP protection now comes from ILPA's templates and from side letters. That puts more of the transparency burden on the client team."

Don't say this

"Reverse solicitation is an easy way round EU marketing rules." Since August 2021, a subscription within 18 months of pre-marketing counts as marketing [S299]. Calling it a loophole signals you would be a compliance risk.

What is happening right now

The stories from the last six months that matter to KKR, its clients and its London teams.

The six months in one paragraph@@n-summary@@

KKR is having a record year while parts of its industry wobble. That tension is the story an interviewer will want you to hold in your head.

KKR raised $34bn of new money in Q2 2026 and $133bn over the 12 months to 30 June, and manages $796bn [S330] CONFIRMED. Co-CEO Scott Nuttall said: "We expect a record fundraising year for the firm" [S362] REPORTED. Two flagship funds closed: North America Fund XIV at about $23bn in April and Global Infrastructure Investors V at $19.2bn in August [S335, S334] CONFIRMED. The private wealth funds (K-Series) reached $42bn [S330] CONFIRMED. Meanwhile wealthy individuals asked to pull more than $20bn out of private credit funds in Q1, and several managers, KKR among them, limited withdrawals [S337, S338] REPORTED. Regulators kept opening private markets to ordinary savers (US 401(k) proposal, SEC accredited investor proposal, UK Pension Schemes Act 2026) while rewriting fund-manager rules (AIFMD II, the new UK AIFM regime) [S342, S275, S346, S344, S345]. Inside KKR, the founders' special control rights end by 31 December 2026 at the latest, and KKR settled a $250m civil case with the US Department of Justice in August [S332, S349] CONFIRMED.

KKR's scoreboard in four charts@@n-numbers@@

For a client team, these are the numbers that matter most: how much KKR manages, how much it raised, and how fast the wealth channel grows. AUM (assets under management) is all the money KKR looks after. "New capital raised" is the money clients committed in the period: the direct output of KCS's work INFERRED.

Why this matters

The fastest-growing line is the wealth channel: K-Series AUM rose 68% in a year, from $25bn to $42bn [S330] CONFIRMED. From Q2 2026 KKR also reports K-Series private equity performance fees (about $160m in Q2) inside Fee Related Earnings, which makes wealth profits look more like steady fees [S332] CONFIRMED. Next results: 9 November 2026 [S333] REPORTED.

KKR's house view in plain English@@n-houseview@@

Henry McVey is KKR's Head of Global Macro and Asset Allocation and CIO of its Balance Sheet [S360] CONFIRMED. His team's outlooks are KKR's public "house view": what the firm thinks about the economy. Clients read them, and client teams use them in meetings INFERRED. KKR's head of talent acquisition told Fortune that KKR wants candidates who "understand how the macro environment is affecting investors" [S393] REPORTED. These two documents are how you show that.

Dec 2025: "Outlook for 2026: High Grading"

The economy is fine but the cycle is late. Do not run from risk; upgrade what you own, how it is financed and who you deal with, because upgrading is cheap today. "Using an education analogy, we think a B is an A in this environment, but a C could be an F." Calls include: create your own returns through operational improvement; favour firms that use AI to grow margins; "We want to own more Asia at this point in the cycle"; own "collateral-based cash flows" because inflation has a higher "resting heart rate" [S361] CONFIRMED.

Jun 2026: "The Divergence Conundrum"

"The cycle continues, but the rules of the game are changing." The economy moves from "a low-cost, efficiency-first model" to one where "redundancy, reliability, resilience, and control carry a higher premium". Some sectors attract capital (AI, productivity, national security); others struggle (housing, lower-income consumers, rate-sensitive sectors). "For investors, the implication is not to avoid risk, but to be more disciplined in how that risk is owned" [S360] CONFIRMED.

Other calls worth knowing from the mid-year update [S360] CONFIRMED: since ChatGPT launched, S&P 500 real revenue per worker is up about 8% after 20 years of no growth; goods inflation should settle about 100 basis points (1 percentage point) above pre-pandemic levels; stocks and bonds diversify each other less; in Europe KKR favours infrastructure, defence, grids, logistics and the periphery (Spain, Italy, Poland), not just a weak Germany; and manager selection "is a bigger part of returns" when results vary more between managers.

Say this in the interview

"KKR's mid-year outlook says the cycle continues but the rules are changing, and that manager selection matters more when returns diverge. That is a fundraising argument as much as a macro view: it explains why capital is concentrating in large platforms like KKR."
